passages.title: Instruments That Argue
text: It is customary to treat scientific instruments as neutral windows: the telescope merely extends the eye, the thermometer merely registers what was already there. On this picture, theory lives in the minds of scientists and in the pages of journals, while instruments are passive servants whose only virtue is accuracy. I want to suggest that this picture has the relationship backward. Instruments are not servants of theory so much as condensed arguments, and a great deal of what a scientific community believes is stored in its equipment rather than in its explicit doctrines.

Consider the early thermometer. Before anyone could measure temperature, someone had to decide that the expansion of a liquid in a sealed tube tracked something real and uniform, and that equal increments of expansion corresponded to equal increments of heat. These were not observations; they were commitments, and contested ones. Different liquids expanded at different rates, and for decades makers disagreed about which substance told the truth. When mercury eventually won, it won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity. Yet once mercury thermometers filled laboratories, the assumptions built into them became invisible. A student reading a scale was, without knowing it, endorsing a theory of heat she could not have stated.

This is why I find it misleading to say that experiments test theories while instruments merely collect data. Every reading is already shaped by choices about what counts as a signal and what counts as noise, and those choices were made by craftsmen and committees long before the experiment began. When a new result conflicts with an established one, scientists rarely blame the instrument first, not because instruments are infallible but because doubting them would mean reopening settled arguments that no one remembers having.

None of this implies that science is arbitrary. Embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined, and the history of science contains many episodes in which a discrepancy finally forced someone to ask what an instrument had been taking for granted. My claim is more modest: the rationality of science is partly a rationality of things. To understand why a field believes what it does, we should read its catalogs of apparatus as carefully as we read its theories.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Instruments are neutral windows that extend human perception.
Paragraph 1 presents this as the customary view the author rejects.
Instruments embody theoretical commitments that often go unexamined.
Correct: paragraph 1 calls instruments condensed arguments, and paragraphs 2-4 develop how their assumptions become invisible.
Scientific conclusions are arbitrary because instruments are biased.
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that science is arbitrary.
Mercury thermometers were less accurate than earlier designs.
Paragraph 2 never compares accuracy; it says mercury's fidelity was assumed, not proven.
qs.x: The thesis comes in paragraph 1: instruments are condensed arguments that store a community's beliefs, and paragraphs 2 to 4 show those built-in assumptions becoming invisible. The neutral-window view is the position the author argues against, and the arbitrariness reading overshoots, since paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary and that hidden assumptions can be examined.

qs.q: According to the passage, mercury became the standard thermometric liquid partly because it:
o: had been proven to expand uniformly with heat
Paragraph 2 says no one had proven mercury's fidelity.
was cheaper than any competing liquid
Cost is never mentioned in paragraph 2; this is outside information.
was endorsed after a decisive experiment
Paragraph 2 describes decades of dispute, not a decisive experiment.
was convenient to work with
Correct: paragraph 2 says mercury won partly because it was convenient, not because its fidelity was proven.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says mercury won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity. That rules out the tempting proof answer, which is the exact opposite of the text. Cost is never mentioned, so choosing it brings in outside assumptions the passage does not support.

qs.q: The author mentions a student reading a thermometer scale primarily to illustrate that:
o: users can unknowingly accept its assumptions
Correct: paragraph 2 says the student endorsed a theory of heat she could not have stated.
students were poorly trained in the theory of heat
Paragraph 2's point is about invisible assumptions, not inadequate teaching.
thermometers were too difficult for beginners to read
Nothing in paragraph 2 suggests the scale was hard to read.
early mercury thermometers gave inaccurate readings that misled the scientists who relied on them
Paragraph 2 never claims the readings were wrong, only that assumptions were hidden.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 ends with a student who, by reading a scale, endorses a theory of heat she could not have stated. The example shows assumptions passing quietly into users. It does not show bad training or wrong readings: the author never says the readings were inaccurate, only that the commitments behind them went unseen.

qs.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
o: Discrepancies sometimes force scientists to examine what instruments assume.
Paragraph 4 affirms this directly.
Scientists tend not to blame instruments first when results conflict.
Paragraph 3 makes exactly this claim.
Because instruments embed prior choices, scientific results cannot be rationally trusted.
Correct: paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary and its embedded assumptions can be examined.
Catalogs of apparatus deserve study alongside scientific theories.
Paragraph 4 ends by recommending this.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary, that embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined, and that science has a rationality of things. So the author would reject the claim that embedded choices make results untrustworthy. The other three statements restate claims the author makes in paragraphs 3 and 4, so the author would agree with them.

qs.q: Which historical finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Two rival thermometer designs gave identical readings under every condition tested.
Agreement between designs says nothing about hidden commitments in paragraph 2's sense.
Scientists facing a surprising result usually suspected their instruments first and rebuilt them before rechecking the theory.
This contradicts paragraph 3's claim that instruments are rarely blamed first.
A measurement dispute ended when one lab's apparatus was adopted, though the question was never resolved.
Correct: it shows a commitment settled by equipment rather than argument, as paragraphs 2-3 describe.
Textbooks of the period stated every assumption built into common instruments, so none went unexamined.
This undercuts paragraph 2's claim that the assumptions became invisible.
qs.x: The author argues that equipment can settle commitments that argument never settled and that then go unexamined (paragraphs 2 and 3). A dispute that ended because one design was adopted, while the real question stayed open, is exactly that pattern. Identical readings from rival designs say nothing about hidden assumptions, since both could share the same unexamined commitment.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's view of instruments?
o: A test whose rubric quietly encodes one view of intelligence
Correct: like paragraph 2's thermometer, the tool carries an unstated theory its users endorse unknowingly.
A road map that has become outdated as new highways were built
This is a simple accuracy problem, not an embedded theoretical commitment.
A microscope whose scratched lens blurs every image it produces, so that every observer who uses it notices the flaw
A defect causes error; the author's point concerns hidden assumptions, not damage.
A translator who openly adds her own commentary in brackets
The additions are explicit, whereas paragraph 2 stresses assumptions that are invisible.
qs.x: The author's point is that a tool can carry an unstated theory that its users accept just by using it, like the thermometer in paragraph 2. A rubric that quietly encodes one definition of intelligence fits this. The scratched lens is tempting, but it is a physical defect that causes error, not a hidden theoretical commitment.

passages.title: Monkeys in the Margins
text: Open almost any illuminated psalter from the late thirteenth or fourteenth century and you will find, at the edges of the sacred text, a riot of improbable creatures: rabbits jousting on horseback, monkeys playing bagpipes, knights fleeing from snails, a bishop with the hindquarters of a dog. Modern viewers delight in these marginal images, and modern scholars have often explained them as a kind of licensed rebellion, the place where the restless imagination of the illuminator escaped the solemn control of the Church.

The rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes. We prefer our medieval artists to be secret ironists, winking at us across the centuries. But the evidence fits it poorly. Many of the most extravagant margins appear in books commissioned by wealthy and devout patrons, often for private prayer, and there is little sign that those patrons were scandalized. Some images respond closely to words on the same page, punning on a phrase or illustrating a verse in absurdly literal fashion. A rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion.

A better account begins with how such books were used. Devotional reading was slow, repetitive, and meant to be memorized. Medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind, and a reader who returned to the same psalm daily needed something to anchor her place and hold her attention. The margins, on this view, are not an escape from devotion but one of its tools: a set of hooks for wandering minds, a way of making the familiar strange enough to be noticed again.

I do not claim that every marginal image had a pious function, or that illuminators never laughed at their betters. Humor and devotion were not opposites for medieval readers, and a single image could amuse and instruct at once. What I resist is the assumption that the center and the margin of the page stood for opposed worlds. They were made by the same hands, paid for by the same purses, and read by the same eyes.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: catalog the most common creatures found in medieval margins
Paragraph 1 lists creatures only as an opening example, not as the passage's aim.
argue that medieval illuminators had no sense of humor
Paragraph 4 says illuminators did sometimes laugh and that humor and devotion coexisted.
show that the Church tightly censored illuminated psalters
The passage never describes censorship; paragraph 2 notes patrons were not scandalized.
challenge the view that marginal images were rebellious and propose a devotional role
Correct: paragraph 2 disputes the rebellion thesis and paragraph 3 offers the memory-aid account.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that the rebellion thesis fits the evidence poorly, and paragraph 3 offers a better account: the margins as memory aids for devotion. The list of creatures in paragraph 1 is only a hook. The claim that the author denies humor is wrong, because paragraph 4 says humor and devotion could coexist in one image.

qs.q: The remark that 'a rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion' serves mainly to:
o: suggest that patrons secretly shared the illuminators' rebellious aims and paid to see them expressed
Paragraph 2 offers no evidence of secret shared rebellion; it doubts rebellion altogether.
highlight a tension between the rebellion thesis and evidence about patronage
Correct: paragraph 2 uses it to show that devout patrons' approval fits poorly with rebellion.
prove that marginal images had no meaning beyond decoration
Paragraph 3 assigns the images a real function as memory aids.
concede that the rebellion thesis is mostly correct despite the evidence about who paid for the books
The remark is ironic criticism, not a concession to the thesis.
qs.x: The line is ironic. Paragraph 2 has just said that devout, wealthy patrons commissioned and approved these margins, and calling that a rebellion shows how badly the thesis fits those facts. It is not a concession, and it does not hint that patrons were secretly rebellious. It treats the patronage evidence as working against any rebellion at all.

qs.q: According to the passage, medieval writers on memory recommended:
o: reading a psalm only once to preserve its freshness
Paragraph 3 says devotional reading was repetitive, returning to the same psalm daily.
vivid, even grotesque images to fix ideas
Correct: paragraph 3 states this advice directly.
removing images from books meant for serious study
Paragraph 3 says images were recommended, not removed.
restricting illustrations to scenes from scripture so that readers would not be distracted
Paragraph 3 endorses grotesque images, not only scriptural scenes.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind. This is a detail question, so the answer has to be stated in the text. Paragraph 3 also says devotional reading was repetitive and daily, which rules out reading a psalm only once.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Further margins that pun on words written on the same page
Paragraph 2 cites such puns as evidence for the author's view.
More extravagant margins in books that were made for private prayer than in books made for public worship
Paragraph 2 already uses this pattern to support the author.
Some marginal images that were clearly meant to be funny to readers of the time, such as animals in clerical dress
Paragraph 4 concedes humor and says it coexisted with devotion.
Records showing devout patrons often demanded that offensive margins be scraped away
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that patrons approved of and were not scandalized by the margins.
qs.x: The author's case against rebellion rests on paragraph 2: devout patrons paid for and approved the margins and were not scandalized. Records of patrons demanding that offensive images be scraped away would attack that premise directly. Funny images do not weaken the argument, since paragraph 4 already grants that humor and devotion went together.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward scholars who hold the rebellion thesis is best described as:
o: skeptical, seeing modern taste more than evidence
Correct: paragraph 2 says the thesis flatters our own tastes and fits the evidence poorly.
admiring, since they first noticed the marginal images
Paragraph 2 criticizes the thesis rather than praising its holders.
contemptuous, dismissing any reading of medieval humor
Paragraph 4 accepts that the images could amuse, so dismissing humor is too extreme.
neutral, presenting their view without evaluating it or offering an alternative account
Paragraph 2 openly argues that the evidence fits the thesis poorly.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes and that the evidence fits it poorly. That is reasoned skepticism. Contemptuous is too extreme: the author calls the thesis appealing and in paragraph 4 accepts that illuminators sometimes laughed, so the author does not dismiss medieval humor.

passages.title: The Grammar of Hearsay
text: In a number of the world's languages, including Turkish, Quechua, and Tuyuca, a speaker cannot simply say that it rained last night. The grammar demands that the sentence also mark how the speaker knows: whether she saw the rain, inferred it from wet streets, or was told about it by someone else. Linguists call this feature evidentiality, and it has attracted a good deal of romantic speculation. Surely, the thinking goes, speakers of such languages must be more scrupulous about truth, more careful to distinguish knowledge from rumor, than those of us who can assert anything without citing our sources.

The speculation is understandable but, I think, mistaken in an instructive way. Obligatory marking does not make speakers more honest; it makes a certain kind of information routine. When every sentence must carry an evidential, choosing one becomes as automatic as choosing a verb tense in English, and automatic choices are not moral achievements. A speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, just as an English speaker can use the past tense to describe events that never happened. The grammar specifies what must be said, not whether what is said is true.

Nor is it clear that languages without grammatical evidentials leave speakers unable to track sources. English speakers have an abundant toolkit: apparently, I hear that, they say, I saw it with my own eyes. The difference is that in English such expressions are optional, and their presence is therefore noticeable. Paradoxically, this may give them more rhetorical force than their grammatical counterparts. When an English speaker goes out of her way to say she saw something herself, listeners take note precisely because she did not have to.

What evidential systems do reveal is that languages differ in which distinctions they make compulsory, and compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to in the moment of speaking. That is an interesting claim about habit and attention. It is not a claim about virtue, and conflating the two tells us more about our wish to find moral lessons in grammar than about grammar itself.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's central claim?
o: Languages with evidentials produce more honest speakers than other languages.
Paragraph 2 calls this romantic speculation mistaken.
English speakers cannot express how they know what they report.
Paragraph 3 lists many English expressions for doing exactly that.
Obligatory evidential marking shapes attention but does not make speakers more truthful.
Correct: paragraph 2 denies the honesty claim and paragraph 4 limits the effect to habit and attention.
Grammar has no effect at all on what speakers notice.
Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions do shape what speakers attend to.
qs.x: The author rejects the romantic idea that evidentials make speakers more honest (paragraph 2). Paragraph 4 then says that compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to. So the central claim has two parts: an effect on attention, but none on truthfulness. Saying grammar has no effect at all is too strong, because paragraph 4 grants the effect on attention.

qs.q: The comparison between evidentials and English verb tense in paragraph 2 is used to show that:
o: evidentials and tense are learned at the same age
Paragraph 2 says nothing about acquisition age.
English tense is a hidden form of evidentiality that speakers use without noticing
Paragraph 2 treats tense as an analogy, not as an evidential system.
a grammatical requirement does not guarantee that the content is true
Correct: paragraph 2 notes one can use the past tense for events that never happened, and likewise lie with an evidential.
speakers choose tenses more carefully than evidentials, since tense errors are noticed more readily
Paragraph 2 says both choices become equally automatic.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes that English speakers can use the past tense for events that never happened, just as one can mark a lie as witnessed. A grammatical requirement fixes the form of a sentence, not whether it is true. The analogy does not say English tense is a kind of evidential, and paragraph 2 says both choices are equally automatic.

qs.q: According to the passage, optional source expressions in English may:
o: carry extra rhetorical force because speakers did not have to use them
Correct: paragraph 3 says listeners take note precisely because the speaker did not have to.
be ignored by listeners because they are so common
Paragraph 3 says their presence is noticeable, not ignored.
be grammatically required in formal speech
Paragraph 3 calls these expressions optional in English.
convey less information than grammatical evidentials, because listeners treat them as mere style
Paragraph 3 suggests they may be more forceful, not less informative.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says optional English expressions like 'I saw it with my own eyes' get noticed precisely because the speaker did not have to use them. This may give them more rhetorical force than grammatical evidentials. The tempting idea that common expressions get ignored contradicts the text, which says their presence is noticeable.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would expect a Quechua speaker who wanted to deceive a listener to:
o: be prevented by the grammar from stating the falsehood
Paragraph 2 says grammar specifies what must be said, not whether it is true.
be forced to use a hearsay marker for any false claim
No rule in paragraph 2 ties falsehood to the hearsay marker.
be detected automatically by native listeners
The passage never claims evidentials expose lies to listeners.
be able to mark a false claim as directly witnessed
Correct: paragraph 2 says a speaker can mark a claim as witnessed while lying about it.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, because grammar specifies what must be said, not whether it is true. So a deceptive Quechua speaker could simply use the witness marker. Nothing in the passage says the grammar prevents lies or that listeners can automatically detect them.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's position?
o: Children acquire evidential markers later than basic verb tenses.
Acquisition timing does not bear on paragraph 2's claim about honesty.
In deception tasks, speakers of evidential languages lie far less often than matched speakers of other languages.
Correct: this ties evidential grammar to honesty, the link paragraphs 2 and 4 deny.
English speakers use expressions like 'apparently' very frequently.
Frequency of English source expressions does not test the honesty claim.
Speakers of evidential languages sometimes lie using the witness marker, especially when talking with strangers.
This supports paragraph 2, which says exactly this can happen.
qs.x: The author denies that evidential grammar makes speakers more honest (paragraphs 2 and 4). A controlled study showing that speakers of evidential languages lie far less than matched speakers would support the very link the author rejects. Lying with the witness marker is the case paragraph 2 describes, so that finding would support the author, not challenge the view.

qs.q: The claim in paragraph 2 that 'automatic choices are not moral achievements' depends on which assumption?
o: Most speakers of evidential languages are dishonest when they are not required to mark their sources.
Paragraph 2 makes no claim that speakers are dishonest, only not more honest.
Moral credit requires something like deliberate effort rather than habitual compliance.
Correct: paragraph 2 denies credit to evidential choices precisely because they are routine, which presumes credit needs deliberation.
English has a complete grammatical evidential system.
Paragraph 3 says English expressions are optional, not grammatical evidentials.
Habitual behaviors cannot affect what speakers attend to, even when the habit is repeated thousands of times daily.
Paragraph 4 says compulsory habits do shape attention.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says evidential choices are not moral achievements because they are automatic. That reasoning works only if moral credit needs something like deliberate effort, not habit. The assumption is not that speakers are dishonest; the author says only that they are not more honest. Paragraph 4 also says habit does shape attention.

passages.title: In Defense of the Vestibule
text: Modern residential design has been at war with the in-between. Open-plan living erased the hallway, the parlor, and the pantry in the name of light and flow, and the vestibule, that small chamber between the front door and the house proper, has nearly vanished from new construction. Architects who remove it are not careless; they see wasted square footage, a dark box that serves no function except to be passed through. In a market that prices homes by area, a room designed for passing through looks like an indulgence.

But the vestibule's function was never primarily spatial. In colder climates it served as an airlock, keeping winter out of the main rooms, and that practical role is real. Its deeper work, however, was social. A vestibule allowed a household to receive a visitor without fully admitting them, to sign for a parcel, decline a salesman, or greet a neighbor while keeping the life of the house out of view. It staged the passage from public to private as a sequence rather than a single step, and in doing so gave both host and guest a moment to adjust their manners.

When the front door opens directly onto the living room, that sequence collapses. Every arrival becomes an intrusion or a full admission; there is no intermediate state. Residents compensate in other ways, with doorbell cameras, with conversations conducted through a half-opened door, with a reluctance to answer at all. These improvisations suggest that the need the vestibule served did not disappear when the room did. It was merely left to be met badly.

I am not arguing that every house needs a small dark room by its front door, nor that older homes were socially superior. Many were built around rigid hierarchies of class and gender that no one should wish to restore. My point is narrower. Architecture encodes assumptions about how people meet, and when we judge rooms only by how much they hold, we lose sight of what they do. Some of the most useful spaces in a building are the ones in which nothing seems to happen.

qs.q: According to the passage, architects remove vestibules mainly because they regard them as:
o: relics of rigid class and gender hierarchies
Paragraph 4 raises hierarchies as the author's own concession, not architects' reason.
ineffective at keeping cold air out of the house
Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real.
unpopular with visitors who dislike waiting
The passage never mentions visitors' dislike as architects' reason.
wasted area whose only function is to be passed through
Correct: paragraph 1 says architects see wasted square footage that serves only for passage.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says architects see the vestibule as wasted square footage, a dark box whose only function is to be passed through. The hierarchy point is tempting, but it is the author's own concession in paragraph 4, not the architects' reason. Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real, so architects do not reject the vestibule for failing to keep out cold.

qs.q: The author mentions doorbell cameras and conversations through a half-opened door in order to:
o: praise technology for replacing outdated rooms
Paragraph 3 calls these improvisations a bad way of meeting the need.
show that the social need the vestibule met persists and is met with poor substitutes
Correct: paragraph 3 says the need did not disappear but is now met badly.
argue that residents have become less friendly toward visitors than they were in earlier generations
Paragraph 3 attributes the behavior to design, not to a change in character.
prove that vestibules improved home security
Paragraph 2 frames the vestibule's role as social, not as security.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says that without a vestibule, residents make do with doorbell cameras, half-opened doors, or not answering at all, and concludes that the need did not disappear but is now met badly. The examples are evidence that the social need persists. They are not praise for technology, and the author blames design, not a change in residents' character.

qs.q: Which function of the vestibule does the author consider most important?
o: Keeping winter air out of the main rooms
Paragraph 2 calls the airlock role real but secondary.
Staging the passage from public to private as a social sequence
Correct: paragraph 2 calls this its deeper work, beyond the spatial role.
Providing extra storage near the front door
Storage is never mentioned as a vestibule function.
Increasing a home's market value by area
Paragraph 1 says pricing by area is why vestibules look wasteful.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real but calls the vestibule's deeper work social: staging the passage from public to private as a sequence. The question asks what the author ranks highest, so the word 'deeper' decides it. Keeping out winter air is a true function in the passage, but the author treats it as secondary.

qs.q: The concession at the start of paragraph 4 serves primarily to:
o: admit that the argument of paragraph 3 was mistaken
Paragraph 4 keeps paragraph 3's argument while limiting its scope.
argue that open-plan homes are socially superior
Paragraph 4 only denies that older homes were superior; paragraph 3 says open plans meet the social need badly.
recommend a vestibule in every new house
Paragraph 4 explicitly says not every house needs one.
narrow the claim so it is not read as nostalgia for older social arrangements
Correct: paragraph 4 rejects restoring old hierarchies and says the point is narrower.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens by saying that not every house needs a vestibule and that older homes were not socially superior, since many reflected rigid class and gender hierarchies. This narrows the claim so it is not read as nostalgia. It does not take back paragraph 3's argument, and it does not suggest a vestibule in every house.

qs.q: Which design would the author most likely praise?
o: A deep, sheltered entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in
Correct: it restores the intermediate state between public and private described in paragraph 2.
An entry converted into a closet to maximize storage space and leave more room for the living area
This judges space by what it holds, the habit paragraph 4 criticizes.
A front door opening straight into the kitchen for efficiency
Paragraph 3 says direct entry collapses the social sequence.
A glass-walled facade that makes the interior fully visible so that callers and residents can see each other before speaking
Paragraph 2 values keeping the life of the house out of view.
qs.x: The author values a space that lets residents receive callers without fully admitting them, an in-between state between public and private (paragraph 2). A deep entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in restores that. Turning the entry into a closet judges space by what it holds, the habit paragraph 4 criticizes.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the author's claim in paragraph 3?
o: Doorbell cameras are more common in homes without vestibules than in older homes that kept them.
This fits paragraph 3's claim that residents compensate with such devices.
Vestibules reduce winter heating costs in cold climates.
This concerns the airlock role from paragraph 2, not the social claim.
Residents of homes with and without vestibules answer the door equally often and with equal ease.
Correct: paragraph 3 claims the need persists and is met badly; equal ease suggests no unmet need.
Many old homes with vestibules reflected class hierarchies.
Paragraph 4 already concedes this point.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims the social need the vestibule met still exists and is now met badly. If people in homes with and without vestibules answered the door equally often and felt equally at ease, there would be no sign of an unmet need. More doorbell cameras in homes without vestibules would support the claim, not weaken it.

passages.title: The Bedside and the Ledger
text: Histories of medicine like to stage a duel. On one side stands the old physician, who reads each patient as a singular case and trusts the trained intuition of his fingertips. On the other stands the statistician, who counts outcomes across hundreds of patients and lets the numbers speak. In the triumphal version of the story, the ledger wins, superstition retreats, and modern medicine is born. I think this version gets the winner right and the battle wrong.

Consider the Parisian physician Pierre Louis, who in the 1830s tallied the courses of pneumonia patients bled early or late and concluded that bloodletting did far less good than his colleagues believed. Louis is usually cast as the hero of the duel. Yet his opponents did not object to counting as such; many of them counted constantly, recording pulses, temperatures and fluid losses. What they resisted was the claim that an average drawn from many bodies could tell a physician what to do with the one body in front of him. That objection was not superstition. It was a serious question about how a general truth becomes a particular decision, and it has never been fully answered.

What the numerical method actually changed was not the amount of knowledge but its address. Before Louis, medical authority lived in the person of the experienced practitioner, who could not easily be contradicted by anyone who had not stood at the same bedsides. After him, authority increasingly lived in tables that anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend. The ledger made medical knowledge portable, cumulative and public. That is a genuine achievement, but it is an achievement in the social organization of knowledge, not a victory of reason over unreason.

Seeing the change this way matters because the old question returns whenever we forget it. A clinician who applies a trial's average result to a frail ninety-year-old patient who resembles no one in the trial is facing exactly the difficulty Louis's critics raised. The honest response is neither to discard the ledger nor to worship it, but to admit that every application of a statistic to a person is an act of judgment, and to train that judgment as carefully as we once trained the fingertips.

qs.q: The author's central claim about the rise of the numerical method is that it primarily:
o: proved that clinical intuition had always been a form of superstition
Paragraph 2 explicitly denies that the critics' objection was superstition.
increased the total amount of reliable knowledge available to doctors
Paragraph 3 says it changed 'not the amount of knowledge but its address.'
relocated medical authority from individual practitioners to shared, inspectable records
Correct: paragraph 3 says the method changed the 'address' of knowledge, making it portable and public.
ended the use of bloodletting in Parisian hospitals within a decade
The passage reports Louis's conclusion but says nothing about how quickly practice changed.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis directly: the numerical method changed 'not the amount of knowledge but its address,' moving authority from the practitioner's person into tables anyone could inspect. The tempting choice about increasing knowledge is the exact idea that sentence denies, and the superstition choice contradicts paragraph 2's defense of the critics.

qs.q: The author mentions that Louis's opponents 'counted constantly' (paragraph 2) most likely in order to:
o: show that the dispute was about applying averages, not about whether to count
Correct: paragraph 2 says what they resisted was using an average to decide about one body.
suggest that Louis copied his method from his own critics
The passage never says Louis borrowed the method from anyone.
demonstrate that the critics' data on bloodletting were more accurate than the figures Louis relied on
No comparison of data accuracy is made anywhere in the passage.
argue that bloodletting was in fact an effective treatment
The author does not defend bloodletting; the point concerns reasoning from averages.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes the critics counted constantly to show that counting itself was never in dispute; what they resisted was letting an average from many bodies dictate treatment of one body. Watch for choices that read in claims the passage never makes, such as Louis borrowing his method or bloodletting actually working.

qs.q: Which phrase best captures the author's attitude toward the 'triumphal version' of medical history?
o: Complete endorsement of both its conclusion and its framing of the dispute
The author rejects the duel framing as misleading.
Complete rejection, since the old physicians were proved right about bloodletting
The author grants the ledger 'won' and calls it a genuine achievement.
Indifference, since historical narratives cannot affect practice
Paragraph 4 says the framing matters because the old question returns in practice.
Partial agreement with its conclusion but rejection of its framing
Correct: paragraph 1 says it 'gets the winner right and the battle wrong.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 ends with the key line: the triumphal story 'gets the winner right and the battle wrong.' So the author accepts that the ledger won but rejects framing it as reason defeating superstition. Total rejection fails because paragraph 3 calls the method a genuine achievement.

qs.q: Which modern situation most closely parallels the difficulty raised by Louis's critics?
o: Debating whether hospital records should be stored electronically or on paper
Storage format does not involve applying a group average to an individual.
Deciding whether a drug tested only on young adults should be given to a child
Correct: like the frail patient in paragraph 4, the child resembles no one in the trial.
Determining whether a trial had enough participants to detect an effect of the size expected
This concerns the trial's internal validity, not applying its result to one person.
Choosing which journal should publish a large epidemiological study
Publication venue is unrelated to the general-to-particular problem.
qs.x: The critics' problem in paragraph 2 is how a general truth from a group becomes a decision about one person, and paragraph 4 applies it to a frail elder unlike anyone in the trial. A child given a drug tested only on young adults is the same gap. Sample-size questions are tempting but concern whether the trial itself is valid, not how to apply its result.

qs.q: Suppose historians found that, after Louis, junior doctors began successfully challenging senior doctors by citing published tables. How would this affect the author's argument?
o: It would weaken the claim that the critics raised a serious question
Who won arguments does not show the critics' question about averages was frivolous.
It would support the claim that numbers shifted where authority resided
Correct: paragraph 3 argues tables let anyone literate dispute established practitioners.
It would weaken the claim that the ledger made knowledge cumulative
Citing published tables is an instance of knowledge being shared and built upon.
It would have no bearing, since the author discusses only Louis himself
The author makes broad claims about the social organization of medical knowledge.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that after Louis, authority moved into public tables that 'anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend.' Junior doctors winning arguments by citing tables is direct evidence for that shift. It does not weaken the critics' question, because who wins an argument says nothing about whether averages fit individual patients.

qs.q: Which assumption is necessary for the author's recommendation in the final paragraph?
o: Clinical trials systematically exclude elderly patients on purpose to make their results look better
The example needs only that some patients differ from trial populations, not deliberate exclusion.
Fingertip diagnosis was more accurate than statistical diagnosis
The author never ranks the accuracy of the two methods.
Most clinicians already worship statistical averages
The author warns against worship but does not assume most clinicians do it.
Skill in applying statistics can be trained.
Correct: the author urges us to 'train that judgment,' which presumes it is trainable.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 recommends that we 'train that judgment' in applying statistics, which only makes sense if such judgment can be improved by training. A necessary assumption is one the argument collapses without. The claim about deliberate exclusion of the elderly is tempting but goes too far: the example needs only that some patients differ from trial populations.

passages.title: What the Unbroken Shot Hides
text: Among critics who care about such things, there persists a moral hierarchy of film technique. The long take, a single shot that runs uncut for minutes, sits near the top: it is said to respect the spectator's freedom, to let time pass as it really passes, and to refuse the manipulation of editing. Montage, the rapid assembly of fragments, sits near the bottom, tainted by its association with propaganda and advertising. The long take is honest; the cut is a lie.

This hierarchy has a distinguished pedigree, but it confuses a style with a virtue. A long take is no less constructed than a montage sequence. Someone chose where the camera stands, what enters and leaves the frame, when the actors move and how long the shot will run before it ends. The absence of visible cuts does not remove the filmmaker's hand; it hides it. If anything, a carefully choreographed long take can be more coercive than editing, because the spectator, believing herself free to look wherever she likes, does not notice how thoroughly her attention has been steered by movement, light and sound.

Nor does montage necessarily deceive. A sequence that cuts between a factory owner's banquet and his workers' meager meal makes its argument openly. The juxtaposition announces itself; the viewer sees that a comparison is being made and can accept or reject it. Editing, in this sense, can be the more candid technique, since it wears its artifice on its surface.

None of this means that the long take lacks distinctive powers. Duration can produce effects nothing else can: the slow accumulation of tension, the boredom that turns into attention, the sense of a world continuing beyond the frame. My objection is only to the claim that these powers are ethical rather than aesthetic. Techniques do not carry morals within them. Honesty in film, as elsewhere, belongs to what is being said and to whether the speaker invites us to see how it is being said, not to the length of the sentences.

qs.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: challenge the idea that long takes are more honest
Correct: paragraph 2 says the hierarchy 'confuses a style with a virtue.'
argue that montage is aesthetically superior to the long take in every kind of film
Paragraph 4 credits the long take with powers 'nothing else can' produce.
trace the historical origins of montage in propaganda films
Propaganda is mentioned only in passing in paragraph 1.
explain the technical difficulty of filming a long take
The passage discusses ethics and style, not technical difficulty.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 states the thesis: the critical hierarchy 'confuses a style with a virtue,' so the long take is not inherently more honest than editing. Saying montage is aesthetically superior overshoots, because paragraph 4 grants the long take powers that nothing else can produce.

qs.q: The banquet example in paragraph 3 is used chiefly to illustrate that:
o: a cut can openly present a comparison the viewer is free to evaluate
Correct: paragraph 3 says the juxtaposition 'announces itself' so the viewer can accept or reject it.
montage is most effective when it depicts economic injustice
The author uses the example for its form, not to rank political subjects.
long takes cannot depict two locations at the same time
The passage never claims this limitation of the long take.
editing always manipulates viewers without their awareness, whatever the director intends
This is the opposite of the point; the example shows editing being candid.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 uses the banquet-versus-workers' meal cut to show that editing can be candid: the comparison 'announces itself,' and the viewer can accept or reject it. The tempting political reading misses that the example is about the form of the argument, not its subject.

qs.q: According to the author, why can a long take be 'more coercive' than editing?
o: Long takes are longer and therefore exhaust the viewer's critical faculties before the scene ends
The author attributes coercion to hidden steering, not to fatigue.
Viewers who feel free to look anywhere fail to notice how their gaze is directed
Correct: paragraph 2 says the spectator 'does not notice' how her attention is steered.
Long takes are mostly used in propaganda and advertising
Paragraph 1 links propaganda to montage, not to the long take.
Editing gives the viewer no choice about where to look, so the viewer notices the director's control
This would make editing more coercive, contrary to the author's point.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the long take hides the filmmaker's hand. A viewer who believes she is free to look anywhere does not notice how movement, light and sound steer her attention. The fatigue choice is tempting because long takes are long, but the passage blames hidden steering, not exhaustion.

qs.q: Which statement would the author be most likely to accept?
o: The long take produces no effects that editing cannot also achieve
Paragraph 4 says duration produces effects 'nothing else can.'
Ethical filmmakers should avoid visible cuts whenever possible
This restates the hierarchy the author rejects.
A documentary that cuts frequently can be more truthful than one that never cuts
Correct: paragraph 4 says honesty lies in what is said, not in shot length.
Film techniques carry inherent moral qualities apart from their use
Paragraph 4 states directly that 'techniques do not carry morals within them.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says honesty belongs to what is said and whether we are shown how it is said, not to technique, so a heavily cut documentary could be the more truthful one. Avoiding cuts restates the hierarchy the author rejects, and denying the long take any unique effects contradicts paragraph 4's list of its powers.

qs.q: Which analogy best reflects the author's reasoning about film technique?
o: A photograph is more honest than a painting because it involves no human choices
The author argues that even unedited images involve many human choices.
Handwritten letters are more sincere than typed ones because they show the writer's effort and care
This ties virtue to a technique, the very move the author rejects.
A live broadcast is more honest than a recording because it cannot be edited
This repeats the long-take hierarchy the author disputes.
Short sentences are not truer than long ones; content decides.
Correct: the final sentence makes this exact comparison to 'the length of the sentences.'
qs.x: The final sentence of paragraph 4 compares shot length to 'the length of the sentences': truth depends on content, not form. An analogy saying short sentences are no more truthful than long ones matches this. The other choices all tie virtue to a technique, which is the reasoning the author attacks.

qs.q: A director makes a ten-minute uncut shot but adds an on-screen note explaining how each movement was rehearsed. How would the author most likely view this?
o: As destroying the long take's distinctive power of unbroken duration and immersion
A note does not shorten the shot or remove its accumulated duration.
As pointless, since long takes are already fully honest
The author denies that long takes are honest by nature.
As increasing the film's candor by showing how its effect is produced
Correct: paragraph 4 locates honesty in inviting us to see 'how it is being said.'
As turning the long take into a form of montage
Adding a note introduces no cuts or juxtaposition of fragments.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 places honesty partly in whether the filmmaker 'invites us to see how it is being said.' A note explaining the rehearsed movements does exactly that, so it makes the shot more candid. Calling it pointless assumes long takes are already honest, which paragraph 2 denies.

passages.title: The Arrow and the Opening
text: Ancient Greek had two words for time. Chronos was time as sequence, the steady march of hours that a water clock could measure. Kairos was time as opportunity, the moment when an action becomes fitting or possible. The word seems to have been used of archery, where it named the narrow gap through which an arrow must pass, and of weaving, where it named the instant when the shuttle can slip through the parted threads. For the teachers of rhetoric, kairos named something no handbook could fully capture: the sense of when to speak, what to say to these listeners in this mood, and when to stop.

Modern instruction in persuasive writing has largely abandoned this idea. Students learn templates: a thesis in the first paragraph, three supporting points, a counterargument, a conclusion that restates the thesis. Such templates have real uses. They make arguments easier to grade and give beginners a scaffold. But they presuppose that a good argument is good everywhere, that its quality is a property of its internal structure rather than of its fit to an occasion.

The older tradition knew better. Gorgias, one of the first professional teachers of rhetoric, reportedly delighted in speaking on any subject an audience proposed, and his showpieces suggest a man more interested in responsiveness than in fixed rules. Even Aristotle, who did more than anyone to systematize rhetoric, insisted that the available means of persuasion must be discovered anew in each case. His categories of appeal were tools for noticing what a situation offered, not formulas for producing speeches in advance.

To restore kairos to the classroom would not mean discarding structure. It would mean teaching students to ask, before they write, who will read this, what those readers already believe, what has just happened that makes the topic urgent or tired, and what would be the wrong thing to say now. These questions cannot be answered by a template, which is precisely why they are worth teaching. An argument that is correct but untimely persuades no one, and an archer who aims perfectly at a closed gap still misses.

qs.q: As the passage uses the term, kairos refers to:
o: the fitting or opportune moment for an action
Correct: paragraph 1 defines it as 'time as opportunity.'
time measured as a steady sequence of hours and days
Paragraph 1 assigns that meaning to chronos, not kairos.
a standard structure for organizing an argument
Templates are a modern practice the author contrasts with kairos.
Aristotle's list of the three types of appeal
Paragraph 3 mentions Aristotle's categories but does not call them kairos.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 contrasts two Greek words: chronos is measured sequence, while kairos is 'time as opportunity,' the fitting moment to act, like the gap an arrow must pass through. The main trap is swapping in chronos's definition, which appears in the same paragraph.

qs.q: The author's main criticism of writing templates is that they:
o: are too difficult for beginning writers to master
Paragraph 2 says templates give beginners a helpful scaffold.
make it harder for instructors to grade student essays
Paragraph 2 says templates make arguments easier to grade.
were invented by Gorgias and so reflect outdated thinking about how persuasion works
Gorgias is presented as interested in responsiveness, not as inventing templates.
treat argumentative quality as independent of the audience and occasion
Correct: paragraph 2 says they presuppose quality is internal rather than fitted to an occasion.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 grants that templates help with grading and give beginners a scaffold. Its objection is that they assume an argument's quality lies in its internal structure, not in how it fits an occasion and audience. Two choices simply reverse the benefits the author concedes.

qs.q: The author refers to Aristotle in paragraph 3 most likely to show that:
o: Aristotle rejected Gorgias's interest in responding to audiences
No disagreement between the two is described.
even the great systematizer of rhetoric treated persuasion as situational
Correct: paragraph 3 says Aristotle held the means of persuasion must be discovered in each case.
systematic approaches to rhetoric inevitably fail
The author says Aristotle's categories were useful tools for noticing.
modern templates are directly derived from Aristotle's categories of ethos, pathos, and logos
The passage draws no line of descent from Aristotle to modern templates.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls Aristotle the thinker who did most to systematize rhetoric, yet says he held that the means of persuasion must be discovered 'anew in each case.' Using him shows that even system-building treated persuasion as situational. Saying systematic approaches inevitably fail overreaches, since his categories are described as useful tools.

qs.q: Which practice would best fit the author's proposal for restoring kairos to the classroom?
o: Requiring every essay to place its thesis in the first sentence
This is a fixed template rule, the approach the author critiques.
Having students rewrite one argument for two audiences with different prior beliefs
Correct: paragraph 4 urges asking who will read and what they already believe.
Grading essays solely on grammar and spelling
Mechanical correctness ignores the occasion and audience entirely.
Having students memorize famous ancient speeches word for word and deliver them before the class
Memorization reproduces past speeches rather than fitting new occasions.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 urges students to ask who will read a piece, what those readers already believe, and what would be wrong to say now. Rewriting one argument for two audiences with different beliefs puts those questions into practice. Memorizing ancient speeches seems true to the classical tradition but copies past occasions instead of fitting new ones.

qs.q: A speechwriter delivers a well-argued case for a budget cut the day after a disaster that the cut would have worsened, and the audience reacts with anger. The author would most likely explain the failure as:
o: proof that the argument's structure was logically flawed
The scenario stipulates a well-argued case; the author separates timing from structure.
evidence that audiences cannot be persuaded by reasoned argument once their emotions are aroused
The author thinks timely arguments can persuade; the issue is fit, not reason.
a result of following Aristotle's categories too closely
The author presents Aristotle's categories as tools for noticing situations.
a failure of timing, regardless of the argument's internal quality
Correct: paragraph 4 says a correct but untimely argument 'persuades no one.'
qs.x: The case is stipulated as well argued, so its structure is not the problem; it came at the worst possible moment. Paragraph 4 says a correct but untimely argument 'persuades no one,' like an archer aiming at a closed gap. The logic-flaw choice ignores that the author treats internal quality and timing as separate.

passages.title: Hot Iron and Reasonable Doubt
text: Few legal practices strike modern readers as more absurd than the medieval ordeal. An accused person might be made to carry a red-hot iron for several paces or plunge an arm into boiling water; if the wound healed cleanly after a few days, God had declared the person innocent. It is tempting to treat such procedures as pure superstition, a grim curiosity from an age before reason. I want to suggest that they were, within their world, a surprisingly shrewd solution to a problem every legal system faces.

That problem is what to do when evidence runs out. Where there were no witnesses and no confession, early medieval courts had few tools for discovering the truth. The ordeal was reserved for exactly such cases. Crucially, it worked through the beliefs of the accused. Someone who believed that God would reveal guilt had strong reason to confess or settle before ever touching the iron, while an innocent person, confident of vindication, had reason to proceed. The ordeal thus sorted defendants by their own expectations, and the mere prospect of it may have extracted many confessions from the guilty.

Records also suggest that a surprisingly large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared. One plausible explanation is that the priests who administered it had considerable discretion, over how hot the iron was, how long it was held and how a healing wound was judged, and may have tended to exonerate those who had shown willingness to proceed. If so, the ordeal was not blind chance but a ritual whose outcome reflected a reasonable inference: those willing to face it were probably innocent.

The system depended entirely on shared belief, and that is why it collapsed. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy to take part in ordeals, partly from theological doubts about demanding miracles of God. Without priests, the ritual lost its authority. English courts turned increasingly to juries of neighbors, a change usually told as progress. Perhaps it was. But we should notice that the jury, too, is a device for producing a verdict when certainty is unavailable, and that it, too, rests on a shared faith, in this case faith in the judgment of ordinary people.

qs.q: According to the passage, ordeals were typically used when:
o: the accused was a member of the clergy
The passage says priests administered ordeals, not that they were the accused.
a jury of neighbors could not agree on a verdict after hearing all the testimony
Paragraph 4 says juries came after ordeals were abandoned.
the crime carried the death penalty and a jury refused to convict
The passage never ties the ordeal to the severity of punishment.
no witnesses or confession were available to settle the case
Correct: paragraph 2 says the ordeal was reserved for cases where evidence ran out.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says ordeals were reserved for cases where evidence ran out: no witnesses and no confession. The jury choice reverses the sequence, because paragraph 4 presents juries as what replaced ordeals after 1215.

qs.q: The author's argument that the ordeal 'sorted defendants by their own expectations' depends on the assumption that:
o: priests were indifferent to the outcome of each ordeal
Paragraph 3 suggests priests used discretion, so indifference is not assumed.
most accused persons sincerely believed God would reveal the truth
Correct: paragraph 2's sorting works only if the accused shared that belief.
guilty people were physically less able to endure pain
The mechanism concerns belief and choice, not pain tolerance.
juries would have reached the same verdicts as ordeals if they had been given the same cases
The argument about sorting does not depend on any comparison to juries.
qs.x: The sorting described in paragraph 2 works only if the accused actually expect God to reveal guilt: the guilty then confess or settle, while the innocent proceed confidently. Without that belief, defendants would have no reason to sort themselves. The priest-indifference choice fails because paragraph 3 suggests priests used discretion.

qs.q: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that ordeal outcomes reflected 'a reasonable inference' rather than chance?
o: The Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy participation in 1215
This explains the ordeal's end, not how its outcomes were reached.
A large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared
Correct: paragraph 3 links frequent acquittals to priests' discretion favoring the willing.
The accused might carry a red-hot iron for several paces
This describes the procedure, not evidence about its outcomes.
English courts later turned to juries of neighbors
This concerns the successor system, not the logic of ordeal verdicts.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 reasons from the high acquittal rate: priests with discretion likely cleared those who had shown willingness to proceed, so outcomes tracked a sensible inference instead of chance. The 1215 council and the later juries concern how the system ended, not how verdicts were reached.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the replacement of ordeals by juries is best described as:
o: enthusiastic, viewing juries as wholly rational
The author stresses that juries also rest on faith.
hostile, arguing that ordeals were more accurate than the juries that replaced them
The author never claims ordeals were more accurate.
indifferent, treating the change as unimportant
The author draws a pointed parallel, which shows interest, not indifference.
cautious, allowing progress but noting a likeness
Correct: paragraph 4 says 'Perhaps it was' and then notes the jury also rests on shared faith.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the move to juries is 'usually told as progress' and answers 'Perhaps it was,' a hedge, before noting that juries also rest on shared faith. That is cautious, qualified acceptance. The hostile choice overreaches, since the author never claims ordeals were more accurate than juries.

qs.q: Which modern practice works most like the mechanism the author attributes to the ordeal?
o: A lie-detector test whose main value is that suspects who believe it works confess beforehand
Correct: like the ordeal in paragraph 2, it works through the suspect's belief in its power.
A DNA test that matches crime-scene samples to a suspect who has denied being present at the scene
DNA evidence works independently of what the suspect believes.
A jury trial in which twelve citizens weigh the evidence
The author presents juries as a successor system relying on faith in ordinary judgment.
A judge's sentencing guidelines based on prior convictions and the seriousness of the current offense
Sentencing guidelines do not elicit confessions through the defendant's beliefs.
qs.x: The ordeal's power in paragraph 2 came through the suspect's belief, which pushed the guilty to confess before the test. A lie detector valued mainly because believing suspects confess beforehand works the same way. DNA testing is tempting as a modern truth-finding tool, but it works no matter what the suspect believes.

passages.title: Reading the Rubbish Heap
text: The public imagines archaeology as a search for treasure: gold masks, painted tombs, the palaces of kings. Practicing archaeologists know that their most informative finds usually come from somewhere far less glamorous. A midden, the heap where a household or village dumped its refuse, can reveal what people ate, which animals they kept, what tools broke and were discarded, and how all of this changed over generations, layer upon layer.

The great virtue of garbage is that it was not meant to be seen. A monument is a message composed for an audience, often for posterity; it tells us what its builders wished to be remembered for. A trash heap tells us what they actually did. A king's inscription may boast of plenty while the village midden from the same decade fills with the bones of animals that were eaten only in famine. Where the two disagree, the archaeologist has good reason to trust the rubbish.

Yet garbage has biases of its own, and they are easy to forget precisely because no one intended them. Bone, pottery and stone survive for thousands of years; wood, textiles, leather and most plant foods rot within decades unless conditions are unusually dry, cold or waterlogged. A midden may therefore suggest a diet dominated by meat and shellfish simply because those remains endure while the grains, roots and greens that fed people daily have vanished. The absence of evidence in a trash heap is often evidence only of decay.

The lesson is not that rubbish is unreliable but that its honesty is of a particular kind. It is free from the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry. A careful archaeologist reads a midden the way a careful historian reads a chronicle: alert to what the source could not have recorded, as well as to what it does. Modern techniques, from sieving for tiny seeds to analyzing chemical residues in pottery, have begun to recover some of what decay erased. But the first discipline remains a habit of mind, the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might a midden overrepresent meat in an ancient diet?
o: Bones survive far longer than most plant remains
Correct: paragraph 3 says bone endures while grains, roots and greens rot.
Ancient people deliberately buried plant waste elsewhere
The passage attributes the bias to decay, not to intentional disposal.
Kings exaggerated meat consumption in their inscriptions
Inscriptions are discussed separately; they do not shape midden contents.
Archaeologists have historically ignored animal bones
If they ignored bones, meat would be underrepresented, not overrepresented.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 explains the bias as uneven decay: bone, pottery and stone last thousands of years, while grains, roots and greens rot. So meat looks dominant only because its remains survive. The choice about archaeologists ignoring bones would make meat look scarcer, the opposite effect.

qs.q: The author contrasts a king's inscription with a village midden (paragraph 2) in order to show that:
o: inscriptions are always false while middens are always true, whatever their date or location
Paragraph 3 says middens have their own biases, so neither is always reliable.
unintended remains can correct the self-presentation of deliberate records
Correct: paragraph 2 says the trash tells what people did, the monument what they wished remembered.
famines were more common than historians once believed
The famine example is hypothetical and illustrates source conflict, not frequency.
villages kept better records than royal courts
A midden is not a record anyone kept; the point is its lack of intention.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a monument shows what its builders wanted remembered, while a trash heap shows what they actually did. Where they conflict, the unintended rubbish can correct the official story. 'Always true' overreaches, since paragraph 3 says middens have biases of their own.

qs.q: The author's statement that rubbish is free from 'the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry' means that middens:
o: were deliberately arranged to mislead later archaeologists
This would be a distortion of intention, which the author says middens lack.
can only be studied using modern chemical analysis
Chemistry here refers to decay, and paragraph 4 calls the first discipline a habit of mind.
are not shaped by a wish to impress yet are filtered by unequal preservation
Correct: paragraph 4 contrasts the absence of intent with the decay described in paragraph 3.
contain toxic substances that endanger excavators
The phrase concerns preservation bias, not physical hazards.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says rubbish is free from 'the distortions of intention' (no one composed it to impress) but not from 'the distortions of chemistry,' meaning the uneven decay of paragraph 3. The deliberate-arrangement choice describes a distortion of intention, which middens lack.

qs.q: Which situation best illustrates the 'habit of mind' the author recommends?
o: Concluding that a site's people ate no vegetables because no plant remains were found in its midden
This treats absence from decay as real absence, the error paragraph 3 warns against.
Trusting a royal inscription over a midden because it is written and was meant to be read by later generations
Paragraph 2 says the archaeologist has reason to trust the rubbish where they disagree.
Excavating only tombs because they contain the most valuable artifacts
The author says the most informative finds come from middens, not treasure.
Concluding that a lack of wooden tools at a dry-rotted site does not prove none were used
Correct: it refuses to mistake what survived for what existed, as paragraph 4 urges.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 names the habit: 'the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed.' Declining to conclude that no wooden tools were used at a site where wood rots shows that habit. Concluding that people ate no vegetables because none were found is the very error paragraph 3 warns about.

qs.q: At a waterlogged site, excavators find a midden full of preserved seeds and textile fragments. Compared with a typical dry midden, this site would most likely:
o: show a diet more dominated by meat and shellfish
Preserving plants would reduce, not increase, the apparent dominance of meat.
be less useful because it lacks a deliberate message
All middens lack deliberate messages; the author counts this as a virtue.
give a fuller picture of daily plant use
Correct: paragraph 3 says waterlogged conditions can preserve normally perishable remains.
contradict the claim that garbage was not meant to be seen by anyone outside the household
Preservation conditions have nothing to do with the original intent behind refuse.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says perishable remains survive only in unusually dry, cold or waterlogged conditions. A waterlogged midden that keeps seeds and textiles therefore offsets the usual preservation bias and gives a fuller picture of plant use and material life. Its plant remains would make meat look less dominant, not more.

passages.title: The Eloquence of Blank Space
text: Historians of cartography once told a simple story about the empty spaces on maps. Medieval and Renaissance mapmakers, the story went, filled unknown regions with sea serpents, cannibal kings and fanciful mountain ranges because they could not bear to admit ignorance; modern cartographers, chastened by science, learned to leave the unknown blank. The blank, on this account, is a badge of honesty, the visible trace of a discipline that has learned to say only what it can verify.

This story flatters us, and it is mostly wrong. Decorative monsters did not usually stand in for ignorance; they often marked waters that sailors had reported as dangerous, and the elaborate cartouches that filled interior spaces advertised the wealth of a patron rather than making a claim about terrain. More importantly, the blank that replaced them was not a neutral confession. When eighteenth-century European mapmakers stripped the interiors of Africa and the Americas of the towns and rivers their predecessors had copied from travelers’ reports, they did not merely subtract error. They also erased knowledge that Indigenous guides and traders had supplied, knowledge that did not count because it had not been measured by a European instrument.

The blank, then, was a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty. It declared that a place was unknown until a particular kind of person had surveyed it, and in doing so it turned inhabited land into an open invitation. A space marked as empty on a map is easier to imagine as empty on the ground; the rhetoric of scientific caution doubled as a rhetoric of availability. It is no accident that the great age of the blank coincided with the great age of territorial claiming.

None of this means that the older maps were better. Their monsters misled, and their borrowed rivers sometimes flowed in impossible directions. The point is that every map makes choices about what counts as knowing, and those choices are never purely technical. To read a map well is to ask not only what it shows but whose testimony it was willing to believe.

qs.q: The author’s central claim about the blank spaces on eighteenth-century maps is that they:
o: reflected a selective standard of evidence with political consequences
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the blank a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty that made land seem available.
were an honest admission of ignorance that improved accuracy and had no political consequences
This is the old story the author rejects in paragraph 2 as flattering and mostly wrong.
were less accurate than the decorated maps they replaced
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that the older maps were better.
were introduced chiefly to lower the cost of engraving the copper printing plates
The passage never discusses production costs; it explains the blank in terms of evidence and power.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis outright: the blank was a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty, and it made inhabited land look available for claiming. Main-idea answers must capture the author's own view, not the view the author sets up to refute. The honest-blank choice is the flattering story paragraph 2 calls mostly wrong.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, the sea monsters on older maps often:
o: concealed the mapmaker’s ignorance of the coastline
That is the old story; paragraph 2 says monsters did not usually stand in for ignorance.
advertised the wealth of the map’s patron
Paragraph 2 says the cartouches, not the monsters, advertised a patron’s wealth.
marked waters sailors reported as dangerous
Correct: Paragraph 2 says monsters often marked waters sailors had reported as dangerous.
recorded information supplied by Indigenous guides to the mapmakers
Paragraph 2 links Indigenous knowledge to interior towns and rivers, not sea monsters.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 separates two decorative features: sea monsters often marked waters sailors reported as dangerous, while cartouches advertised a patron's wealth. Detail questions reward matching the exact noun the passage attaches to each claim. The patron choice is tempting because it sits in the same sentence but describes cartouches, not monsters.

qs.q: The author mentions that older maps had rivers flowing “in impossible directions” most likely in order to:
o: show that travelers' reports were generally unreliable and should have been discarded
The author defends the value of reported knowledge; one flaw is not a verdict on all reports.
concede the flaws of older maps without giving up the main argument
Correct: Paragraph 4 grants the older maps misled, then restates that every map embeds choices about knowing.
argue that instrument-based surveys were unnecessary for producing accurate maps
Paragraph 4 admits older maps erred, which if anything shows measurement had value.
prove that monsters were more trustworthy than rivers
The author says both monsters and borrowed rivers could mislead; no such ranking is made.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens with a concession: older maps misled and their rivers sometimes ran in impossible directions. Authors often concede a point to look fair and then restate their thesis, here that every map makes non-technical choices about what counts as knowing. The concession does not discredit travelers' reports in general, since the author's whole case is that such testimony was wrongly discarded.

qs.q: The claim that it is “no accident” that the age of the blank coincided with territorial claiming depends most on which assumption?
o: Governments ordered mapmakers to erase Indigenous knowledge on purpose.
The author argues from effect, not from a documented deliberate order; this is stronger than needed.
How land is represented can shape how people think about taking it.
Correct: Paragraph 3 argues that land shown as empty is easier to imagine as empty on the ground.
Indigenous reports were always more accurate than European surveys.
The argument concerns which testimony counted, not that one source was always more accurate.
A territory cannot be claimed until it has been fully surveyed.
Paragraph 3 suggests the opposite: unsurveyed blank land invited claims.
qs.x: The 'no accident' claim links two things, maps and territorial claiming, so it needs a bridge: how land is pictured affects how people think about taking it. Paragraph 3 supplies exactly that bridge when it says land shown as empty is easier to imagine as empty on the ground. A deliberate government order would be a stronger claim than the argument requires, and the author never asserts one.

qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author’s account of why interiors were left blank?
o: Some medieval monsters appeared in waters no sailor had ever visited.
This touches a side point in paragraph 2, not the argument about eighteenth-century blanks.
Eighteenth-century survey instruments were more precise than earlier ones.
This is consistent with the passage; it does not explain away the exclusion of testimony.
Eighteenth-century mapmakers often kept Indigenous-reported rivers that no European had measured.
Correct: Paragraph 2 says such knowledge was erased because it lacked European measurement; this contradicts that.
Patrons continued to commission decorated cartouches in that century.
Cartouches are a decorative detail in paragraph 2 and bear little on why interiors went blank.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 explains the blanks by saying Indigenous knowledge was discarded because no European instrument had measured it. If mapmakers routinely kept unmeasured Indigenous-reported rivers, that cause collapses. To weaken an argument, target its central causal claim; the medieval-monster choice touches only a side point about older maps.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author’s view of the cartographic blank?
o: A star chart leaves gaps where no telescope has yet looked.
This matches the naive honest-blank story of paragraph 1, since no available testimony is excluded.
A species database lists a fish as absent from a lake until a credentialed scientist logs it, despite local fishers’ reports.
Correct: Like paragraph 3’s blank, absence here reflects whose testimony counts, not what is actually there.
A tourist map highlights only attractions that paid for advertising.
This resembles the patron-driven cartouches, a minor point, not the blank’s exclusion of testimony.
A weather map shows forecasts but omits last year’s rainfall.
Omitting irrelevant data is not discounting knowledgeable informants, which is the author’s point.
qs.x: The author's point is that a blank records whose testimony was accepted, not simply what is unknown. A database that lists a fish as absent despite local fishers' reports matches this: the absence reflects a credential rule. The star-chart gap is the tempting trap, because there no available testimony is being excluded, which is the honest-blank story of paragraph 1.

passages.title: The Tale Without an Original
text: When nineteenth-century collectors went into the countryside to record folktales, they believed they were rescuing something old and fragile: the authentic voice of the people, preserved by oral tradition and threatened by literacy and the city. Their published volumes presented the tales as found objects, faithfully transcribed. We now know that many collectors polished what they heard, merging versions from different tellers, cutting coarse episodes, adding moral reflections and, in some cases, relying on informants who were themselves well-read members of the middle class.

It is tempting to respond to these revelations with disillusionment, to conclude that the collections are forgeries and that the true folktale lies somewhere behind them, uncontaminated. But this response repeats the collectors’ own error. It assumes that there was once a pure, original version of each tale, and that every later telling is a degradation of it.
