Oral tradition does not work that way. A tale exists only in its performances, and each teller adapts it to an audience, a season and a purpose. There is no first telling to recover, only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale itself.

Seen in this light, the collector who edited a story was not stepping outside tradition but taking part in it. He was one more teller, adapting the material for a new audience, the reading public, as village storytellers had adapted it for the hearth. His version differs from theirs in its medium and its reach, not in its basic relationship to some lost source.

This does not excuse the collectors’ claims of fidelity, which misled readers about what they were getting. The problem was not that they changed the tales; it was that they denied changing them. The honest folklorist today records the variants, names the tellers, and admits her own hand in shaping the record.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the discovery that collectors edited the tales they published?
o: The collections are forgeries that hide the true folktales.
Paragraph 2 rejects this disillusioned response as repeating the collectors’ error.
The editing was harmless because readers knew the tales had been changed.
Paragraph 4 says the claims of fidelity misled readers.
Scholars should reconstruct each tale’s original version.
Paragraph 2 says there is no first telling to recover.
The claims of fidelity were wrong, but the editing itself continued oral tradition.
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the editor one more teller; paragraph 4 faults only the denial of changes.
qs.x: The author splits the verdict: paragraph 4 faults the collectors for claiming fidelity, while paragraph 3 says editing a tale was itself part of oral tradition. Watch for answers that capture only half a two-part position. The 'forgeries' choice is the disillusioned reaction paragraph 2 rejects, because it assumes a pure original that never existed.

qs.q: The phrase “a cloud of variants” in paragraph 2 primarily emphasizes that:
o: no version of a tale is the true original
Correct: Paragraph 2 says no variant has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale.
the tales were vague and hard to transcribe
The image concerns many equal versions, not vagueness of content.
the oldest versions have been lost forever
The author denies there was a single first version to lose.
collectors confused tales from different regions and villages
The phrase describes oral tradition itself, not collectors’ mistakes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a tale exists only in its performances, so there is 'only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others.' The image stresses many equal versions with no privileged original. The 'lost oldest version' choice is tempting but backwards, since the author denies there was ever a single first telling to lose.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, which practice did some collectors engage in?
o: Recording tellers with early sound equipment
The passage never mentions sound recording.
Merging versions told by different storytellers
Correct: Paragraph 1 lists merging versions from different tellers.
Paying storytellers to invent new tales for them
Paragraph 1 describes polishing tales, not commissioning inventions.
Translating foreign tales and passing them off as local
No such practice is described in paragraph 1.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 lists what some collectors did: polished tales, merged versions from different tellers, cut coarse episodes, added morals and used well-read middle-class informants. Merging versions is named directly. The other choices sound like plausible editorial abuses, but none appears in the passage.

qs.q: The author would most likely criticize a modern folklorist who:
o: publishes several variants of a tale with tellers named
Paragraph 4 describes this as the honest folklorist’s practice.
adapts a tale for children and notes in a preface the changes she made
Paragraph 3 treats adapting as tradition; noting changes meets paragraph 4’s honesty standard.
publishes one composite tale as a single teller’s exact words
Correct: Paragraph 4 faults denying changes, which this does by hiding the merging.
describes her own role in shaping the record
Paragraph 4 says the honest folklorist admits her own hand.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 locates the collectors’ fault in denying their changes, not in making them. A folklorist who presents a composite tale as one teller’s exact words repeats that denial. The children’s-adaptation choice is a trap: adapting is acceptable on paragraph 3’s view, and noting the changes meets paragraph 4’s standard of honesty.

qs.q: Which approach is most consistent with the author’s view of oral tales?
o: An editor restores a novel to the text of the author’s original manuscript.
This assumes an authoritative original, the model paragraph 2 says oral tradition lacks.
A scholar seeks the earliest written version of a tale to identify its true form.
Paragraph 2 rejects the idea of a pure first version.
A curator removes later additions from a medieval song collection.
This treats later changes as contamination, the error the author identifies.
A musicologist treats each recorded performance of a traditional ballad as an equally legitimate form of the song.
Correct: This mirrors paragraph 2: the work exists only in performances, none privileged.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 holds that an oral tale has no authoritative original and exists only in performances, none privileged over the others. A musicologist treating every ballad performance as an equally legitimate form of the song applies that view directly. The other three choices all assume an original or earlier form against which later versions count as departures or contamination.

passages.title: Brothers Within the Walls
text: To many economic historians, the medieval craft guild is a textbook cartel. By limiting the number of masters, fixing prices, and forbidding outsiders to sell within the town walls, guilds enriched their members at the expense of consumers and slowed innovation for centuries. The verdict has the clarity of a model, and much evidence supports it.

But the cartel story describes what guilds restricted without explaining what their members believed they were doing. Guild ordinances spend remarkable energy on matters that brought no obvious profit: the inspection of cloth for hidden flaws, the punishment of bakers who sold underweight loaves, the payment of funeral costs for poor brothers, the support of widows. A guild was also a religious brotherhood with its own altar and feast day, and in many towns a unit of the militia and a seat on the council. Membership defined a man's standing in the community, not just his trade.

Seen this way, guild rules expressed an ideal of the 'just price,' one that let an honest craftsman support his household without enriching himself at his neighbors' expense. Competition, in this moral economy, was not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers. Restrictions that look like rent-seeking to a modern economist could look like integrity to a fifteenth-century weaver.

It would be sentimental to stop there. The brotherhood that supported widows also excluded Jews, foreigners, and, increasingly, women who had once practiced trades in their own right; the solidarity inside the walls was built partly on hostility toward those outside them. The point is not that guilds were benign rather than self-serving, but that the two descriptions cannot be pulled apart. Protection of members and exclusion of others were, for the guilds, the same act seen from different sides.

qs.q: According to the cartel view described in paragraph 1, guilds:
o: mainly provided welfare for widows and poor members.
Paragraph 2 raises welfare to show what the cartel story leaves out.
encouraged innovation by protecting skilled craftsmen from cheaper rivals in other towns.
Paragraph 1 says the cartel view holds that guilds 'slowed innovation.'
enriched their members by restricting competition at consumers' expense.
Correct: paragraph 1 says guilds 'enriched their members at the expense of consumers.'
expressed a sincere ideal of the just price.
Paragraph 3 offers this as the author's alternative reading.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 sums up the cartel view: by limiting masters, fixing prices and excluding outsiders, guilds 'enriched their members at the expense of consumers.' The just-price ideal and welfare for widows are the author's additions in paragraphs 2 and 3, offered to complicate the cartel story, so they are not part of that view.

qs.q: The author mentions cloth inspection and funeral payments primarily to:
o: show that guilds pursued aims the profit motive does not explain.
Correct: paragraph 2 calls these 'matters that brought no obvious profit.'
prove that guilds were not cartels at all and never restricted competition.
Paragraph 1 concedes 'much evidence supports' the cartel view; the examples supplement that view rather than refute it.
illustrate how guilds excluded outsiders.
Exclusion is the subject of paragraph 4; these examples concern members' welfare and quality.
explain why guilds eventually disappeared.
The passage never discusses the decline of guilds.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists cloth inspection, underweight loaves, funeral costs and support of widows as 'matters that brought no obvious profit,' showing that the cartel story misses part of what guilds did. The tempting 'prove guilds were not cartels' goes too far: paragraph 1 grants that 'much evidence supports' the cartel view, so the examples supplement it rather than refute it.

qs.q: In the moral economy described in paragraph 3, competition was regarded as:
o: a neutral way of discovering the value of goods in the marketplace.
Paragraph 3 says competition was 'not a neutral mechanism for discovering value.'
a temptation to dishonest practices and underselling.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it 'a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.'
a religious duty owed to the brotherhood.
Religious ties appear in paragraph 2 but are not linked to competition.
the main source of the just price for goods sold in the town.
The just price was protected by restrictions, not by competition (paragraph 3).
qs.x: In paragraph 3's moral economy, competition was 'not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.' The 'neutral mechanism' choice is the modern economist's view that the passage explicitly contrasts with the guild outlook, so it is the reverse of what was asked.

qs.q: What is the main function of the final paragraph?
o: To abandon the moral-economy reading in favor of the cartel model presented in paragraph 1
Paragraph 4 says the two descriptions 'cannot be pulled apart,' so neither replaces the other.
To argue that guilds were mainly benign institutions
Paragraph 4 denies that guilds were 'benign rather than self-serving.'
To introduce new evidence about guild pricing
Paragraph 4 concerns membership and exclusion, not prices.
To argue that protection and exclusion went together
Correct: paragraph 4 says 'it would be sentimental to stop there' and calls the two 'the same act seen from different sides.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens 'It would be sentimental to stop there,' then adds that guild solidarity rested on excluding Jews, foreigners and women, and that protection and exclusion were 'the same act seen from different sides.' It qualifies the sympathetic reading without abandoning it, which rules out the choice that the author returns to the cartel model.

qs.q: Which modern institution most closely resembles the guild as the author portrays it?
o: A licensing board that enforces ethical standards and also limits entry into a profession
Correct: like the guild in paragraphs 2 to 4, it combines care for standards with restricted membership.
An open online community that anyone may join and leave freely without paying fees or meeting standards
Open entry lacks the exclusion that paragraph 4 makes central.
A commodity exchange where prices are set purely by bidding
Pure price competition is what the guild moral economy opposed (paragraph 3).
A charity that gives aid to anyone in need without asking them to meet any standard or join any group
Universal aid lacks the insider-outsider line drawn in paragraph 4.
qs.x: The author's guild combines a real commitment to standards and members' welfare (paragraphs 2 and 3) with restricted entry and exclusion of outsiders (paragraph 4). A licensing board that enforces ethics while limiting entry joins both features. A charity aiding anyone is tempting for its welfare role, but it lacks the insider-outsider line that paragraph 4 makes central.

qs.q: Suppose records showed that a guild loosened its quality inspections whenever it could raise prices without penalty. This would most weaken the claim that:
o: guilds limited the number of masters.
Limiting masters is a cartel feature this finding leaves untouched.
guilds excluded Jews, foreigners and women from becoming masters in the trade.
The finding concerns quality and prices, not membership.
guild rules reflected members' sincere commitment to honest work.
Correct: putting profit ahead of standards undercuts paragraph 3's claim that the rules could express 'integrity.'
guilds served religious and civic roles.
Altars, feasts and militia roles (paragraph 2) are unaffected by inspection practices.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 suggests guild restrictions could reflect 'integrity,' a sincere commitment to honest work and the just price. If a guild relaxed quality inspections whenever it could raise prices safely, profit would be driving its standards, which undercuts that sincerity. Limiting the number of masters is a cartel feature that this finding leaves untouched, even reinforces.

passages.title: Words at Work
text: For much of the history of philosophy, the meaning of a word was thought to be the thing it stood for. 'Apple' meant apples; 'justice' meant some more elusive object that philosophers were charged with locating. The later Wittgenstein proposed a different picture. Words, he suggested, are less like labels than like tools, and their meanings are found in the uses to which they are put within particular activities, which he called language-games. A builder who calls out 'Slab!' to an assistant is not naming an object for contemplation but giving an instruction within a shared task.

Critics have often heard this as a recipe for relativism. If meaning is simply use, and different communities use words differently, then it seems no use can be wrong and no claim can be criticized from outside its own game. This reading, though common, misunderstands the analogy. Games have rules, and a move can be mistaken: one can castle illegally in chess or call a strike when the pitch was wide. To say that meaning lies in use is to say that it lies in a practice with standards of correctness, not in whatever a speaker happens to intend.

The more interesting consequence of the view is not relativism but a diagnosis of confusion. Many apparent disagreements arise when a word migrates from one game to another while carrying the expectations of its first home. When an economist and a theologian argue about whether a gift can ever be truly 'free,' they may not be disputing a fact at all, but talking past each other with a single word that does different work in each of their practices.

The lesson is not that every dispute dissolves under analysis. Some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out. But before we argue, it is worth asking whether we are playing the same game, and whether the word at the center of the quarrel means for our opponent what it means for us.

qs.q: According to the passage, the traditional view held that a word's meaning is:
o: the use it is put to within an activity.
Paragraph 1 attributes this to the later Wittgenstein, as an alternative.
whatever the speaker happens to intend.
Paragraph 2 rejects this as a reading of use-based meaning; it is not the traditional view.
a rule within a shared game.
Rules and games belong to Wittgenstein's picture (paragraphs 1 and 2).
the thing the word stands for.
Correct: paragraph 1 says meaning 'was thought to be the thing it stood for.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 opens with the traditional view: a word's meaning 'was thought to be the thing it stood for,' as 'apple' means apples. Meaning as use within an activity is Wittgenstein's alternative, introduced as a contrast. 'Whatever the speaker intends' is a trap from paragraph 2, where the author rejects it as a misreading of the use view.

qs.q: The examples of illegal castling and a mistaken strike call are offered to show that:
o: games are a poor analogy for language because games have written rules.
The author uses the examples to defend the analogy, saying critics 'misunderstand' it.
meaning grounded in use still allows for mistakes.
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'games have rules, and a move can be mistaken.'
different communities play the same games differently and follow different rules.
Paragraph 2 uses the examples to show standards of correctness, not variation.
umpires and referees decide what words mean.
The examples show that rules exist, not that officials set meanings.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 answers the relativism charge by noting that 'games have rules, and a move can be mistaken,' like illegal castling or a wrong strike call. So meaning grounded in use still has standards of correctness. The choice that games are a poor analogy reverses the author's purpose; the examples defend the analogy against critics who 'misunderstand' it.

qs.q: The author's reply to the charge of relativism would be most weakened if it were shown that:
o: many disputes arise when words move between practices that use them in different ways.
This is the author's own claim in paragraph 3, so it would not weaken the reply.
some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out.
Paragraph 4 already grants this point.
language-games lack any shared standards by which a move can be judged wrong.
Correct: paragraph 2's defense rests on use being 'a practice with standards of correctness.'
builders rarely shout single-word commands.
The builder is only an illustration; its frequency is beside the point (paragraph 1).
qs.x: The author's reply in paragraph 2 depends on use being 'a practice with standards of correctness.' If language-games had no shared standards for judging a move wrong, the reply would collapse and relativism would return. The other choices restate points the author already grants (paragraphs 3 and 4) or attack a mere illustration, so they cannot weaken the argument.

qs.q: Which scenario best illustrates the kind of confusion described in paragraph 3?
o: A doctor and patient read 'chronic' differently
Correct: one word does different work in two practices, so the two talk past each other (paragraph 3).
Two chess players disagree about whether a particular move broke the rules of the game they agreed on
This is a dispute within a single game with shared standards, as in paragraph 2.
Two historians disagree about the date of a battle
Both use 'date' the same way; this is a genuine factual dispute.
A child learns the word 'apple' by being shown an apple
This matches the labeling picture in paragraph 1, not a word moving between practices.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 describes confusion that arises when one word does different work in two practices, so speakers talk past each other, as with 'free' for the economist and the theologian. A doctor's 'chronic' (long-lasting) heard by a patient as 'severe' fits this exactly. Two chess players arguing over a rule is a dispute inside one game with shared standards, which is genuine rather than confused.

qs.q: What does the author ultimately recommend?
o: Treat every disagreement as a misunderstanding about the meanings of the words involved.
Paragraph 4 says 'not that every dispute dissolves under analysis.'
Before arguing, check whether both sides use the key word the same way.
Correct: paragraph 4 urges asking 'whether we are playing the same game.'
Return to defining words by the objects they name.
The author favors use over the labeling view of paragraph 1.
Avoid disputes between different academic fields.
The author asks for clarity about terms, not avoidance of dispute.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 concludes that 'before we argue,' we should ask 'whether we are playing the same game' and whether the key word means the same to both sides. Treating every disagreement as verbal is the overreach the author rules out by saying not 'every dispute dissolves under analysis' and that some disagreements are genuine.

passages.title: The Instructed Child
text: Histories of children's literature tend to follow a plot of liberation. In the beginning, we are told, were the improving tracts of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, in which disobedient children fell into ponds and pious ones died serenely, and in which every story ended in a lesson. Then came Lewis Carroll, whose Alice tumbled into a world of nonsense where the morals were mocked, and children's books were set free to delight rather than instruct.

The plot has its truth. Carroll did parody the moral verses that Victorian children memorized, and the books that followed him gave imagination a standing it had seldom enjoyed. But the liberation narrative mistakes a change in what children's books teach for a change in whether they teach. Walk through the picture-book section of any modern bookstore and you will find books about sharing, about naming one's feelings, about welcoming the new child in class, about the dignity of every kind of family. These books are no less earnest than the tracts they supposedly replaced. They have simply exchanged obedience and piety for empathy and self-acceptance.

This is not a complaint. Adults who write for children are, almost unavoidably, telling them what kind of people to become, and it would be strange to wish otherwise. The trouble with the liberation story is that it lets each generation imagine that its own lessons are not lessons at all but simply the truth, while the moralizing belongs only to the past. The Victorian author who warned against vanity believed he was describing reality, not imposing a value. So, very often, do we.

A more honest history would read the didactic tract and the contemporary picture book side by side, as documents of what different societies hoped their children would be. It would also ask why the books children love most, from Carroll's to the present, so often seem to slip free of whatever lesson the adults intended.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the liberation narrative is that it:
o: exaggerates the harshness of early moral tracts.
The author does not dispute paragraph 1's depiction of the tracts.
gives Lewis Carroll too little credit.
Paragraph 2 affirms Carroll's role; the problem lies elsewhere.
mistakes a change in what children's books teach for an end to teaching.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it confuses a change in what books teach with whether they teach.
ignores the commercial pressures that shaped what publishers would print for children.
Commercial pressures are never discussed in the passage.
qs.x: The author accepts that Carroll changed children's books but says the liberation story confuses a change in what books teach with an end to teaching. Modern picture books still instruct, just about empathy instead of piety. The author does not dispute the description of the old tracts.

qs.q: The author's remark about the Victorian author who warned against vanity, followed by 'So, very often, do we,' suggests that:
o: modern writers also tend to mistake their own values for plain truth.
Correct: paragraph 3 says each generation treats its own lessons as simply the truth.
modern writers warn against vanity more often and more forcefully than Victorian writers did.
The parallel concerns self-perception, not the topic of vanity.
Victorian authors knowingly imposed their values.
Paragraph 3 says the Victorian believed he was describing reality.
readers today reject moral lessons in children's books.
The author describes writers' assumptions, not readers' rejection of lessons.
qs.x: The Victorian thought he was describing reality, not imposing a value; 'So, very often, do we' says moderns make the same mistake about their own lessons. The parallel concerns self-perception, not vanity. It cannot mean Victorians knowingly imposed values, since the passage says the opposite.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward instruction in children's books is best described as:
o: disapproving, since lessons stifle children's imagination and their pleasure in reading.
Paragraph 3 opens by saying 'This is not a complaint.'
nostalgic for the moral clarity of the earlier tracts and their direct lessons.
The author shows no preference for the older lessons.
indifferent, since children ignore lessons anyway.
The author treats the lessons as revealing and worth studying, not ignorable.
accepting of it as nearly unavoidable while urging awareness of it.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls instruction almost unavoidable and faults only self-deception about it.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says 'This is not a complaint' and calls instruction almost unavoidable; the author's objection is only to each generation's blindness to its own lessons. So the attitude is acceptance plus a call for awareness. Disapproval is ruled out by the author's explicit disclaimer.

qs.q: Which research project would the author most likely recommend?
o: Measuring whether modern picture books raise children's empathy scores more than Victorian tracts did
The author's interest is in what books reveal about societies, not their measured effects.
Comparing a Victorian moral tract with a recent picture book as evidence of each era's ideals
Correct: paragraph 4 calls for reading them side by side as documents of each society's hopes.
Cataloging which moral verses Carroll parodied in his books
This narrows to Carroll and misses the comparative aim of paragraph 4.
Surveying parents on which lessons they want books to teach
Paragraph 4 proposes a historical reading of texts, not an opinion survey.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 proposes reading the didactic tract and the modern picture book side by side as documents of what each society hoped its children would be. A comparative historical study of both matches that directly. Measuring empathy effects shifts the focus to outcomes, which the author never asks about.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage most strongly implies that the books children love most:
o: contain no moral content at all.
The sentence says they slip free of intended lessons, not that they lack morals.
were written without any adult intention.
Paragraph 4 says adults intended lessons; the books simply exceed them.
owe part of their appeal to what escapes their authors' intended lessons.
Correct: paragraph 4 notes that favorites seem to slip free of the lessons adults intended.
are mostly nonsense books written in Carroll's tradition of parody.
The sentence spans Carroll to the present without limiting itself to nonsense.
qs.x: The final sentence notes that the most loved books seem to slip free of the lessons adults intended, implying their appeal partly lies in what exceeds those lessons. It does not say they lack morals or adult intention; slipping free of an intended lesson presupposes one existed.

passages.title: Stories Told From the Center
text: Every society that has pushed against an edge has told stories about the edge. In the United States the most famous version was given scholarly form in 1893, when a young historian argued that the availability of open land had shaped the national character, producing individualism, practical ingenuity and a democratic suspicion of inherited rank. The thesis was elegant, and it arrived just as the census office had announced that a continuous line of settlement could no longer be drawn on the map.

That timing deserves more attention than the thesis itself. A myth of the frontier is rarely composed on the frontier. It is composed afterward, in cities, by people who feel the loss of something they never personally possessed. The settlers whose diaries survive wrote mostly about debt, weather, illness and the price of seed. The grand narrative of self-reliance belongs to their grandchildren, who needed an origin story capable of reassuring an industrial and increasingly crowded nation that its virtues had been forged somewhere wider than a factory floor.

Read this way, frontier myths are documents of the center rather than of the margin. They record what a settled society fears it lacks. Where the city feels hemmed in, the myth supplies space; where the corporation dissolves individual achievement, the myth supplies the lone homesteader; where politics feels corrupt, the myth supplies a simpler justice. The people already living on the supposedly open land appear in such stories chiefly as obstacles or as scenery, a revealing absence that tells us whose needs the story serves.

None of this means the myths are merely false. They have real effects, shaping policy, advertising and the private ambitions of people who will never see a prairie. But their truth is the truth of a symptom. To ask whether the frontier really produced self-reliant democrats is to ask the wrong question. The better question is why a nation, at a particular moment, needed so badly to believe that it had.

qs.q: The author's main point is that frontier myths are best understood as:
o: evidence about the anxieties of the settled society that tells them.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls them 'documents of the center' that record what a settled society fears it lacks.
accurate accounts of how open land shaped national character.
Paragraph 4 says asking whether the frontier really did this is 'the wrong question.'
harmless fictions with little effect on public life.
Paragraph 4 says the myths shape policy, advertising and private ambitions.
records written by settlers about their daily hardships.
Paragraph 2 contrasts the settlers' diaries with the later myth composed in cities.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: frontier myths are 'documents of the center rather than of the margin,' recording what a settled society fears it lacks. The tempting choice, that they accurately show how open land shaped character, is the 1893 thesis the author sets aside in paragraph 4 as 'the wrong question.'

qs.q: The author mentions settlers' diaries about debt, weather and seed prices primarily in order to:
o: show that settlers were more self-reliant than historians believed.
The diaries are used to show ordinary worries, not to confirm the myth.
argue that diaries are the most reliable historical sources.
The author uses the diaries as a contrast, not to rank source types.
contrast settlers' actual concerns with the later myth of self-reliance.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the grand narrative 'belongs to their grandchildren,' not the settlers themselves.
explain why the frontier thesis appeared in 1893.
The 1893 timing is tied to the closing of settlement in paragraph 1, not to the diaries.
qs.x: Ask what work a detail does in the argument. The diaries' worries about debt, weather and seed prices show that settlers did not write the grand narrative; paragraph 2 says it 'belongs to their grandchildren' in the cities. The detail is a contrast between lived concerns and later myth, not evidence for settler self-reliance or a ranking of sources.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, people already living on the 'supposedly open land' appear in frontier myths mainly as:
o: heroic models of self-reliance.
Paragraph 3 assigns that role to the lone homesteader, not to existing inhabitants.
the main authors of the stories.
Paragraph 2 says the myths were composed in cities by later generations.
obstacles or scenery.
Correct: paragraph 3 says they appear 'chiefly as obstacles or as scenery.'
victims whose losses the myths mourn.
The passage says their near-absence reveals whose needs the story serves, not that it mourns them.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says existing inhabitants appear 'chiefly as obstacles or as scenery,' and calls this a revealing absence that shows whose needs the story serves. The heroic role goes to the lone homesteader, and the passage never says the myths mourn the inhabitants; their marginal place is evidence that the stories serve the center.

qs.q: In saying that the myths possess 'the truth of a symptom,' the author most likely means that they:
o: reveal real underlying needs even when they misdescribe the past.
Correct: paragraph 4 treats the myths as signs of what a nation 'needed so badly to believe.'
are true only for the generation that first experienced the frontier.
Paragraph 2 says the myths were composed by later generations, not frontier settlers.
describe a disease that weakened the national character.
'Symptom' is a metaphor for what the myth indicates, not a literal claim of illness.
were proven accurate in most details by later historical research.
The author sets aside whether the myth is accurate as 'the wrong question.'
qs.x: A symptom is a real sign of an underlying condition, even if it is not the condition itself. Paragraph 4 says the myths are not merely false and that the better question is why a nation 'needed so badly to believe' them. So their truth lies in what they reveal about present needs, not in accuracy about the past; 'symptom' is a metaphor, not a claim of disease.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Most frontier novels were written by people who had lived on homesteads and farmed the land themselves.
That would cut against paragraph 2's claim that the myth is composed afterward, in cities.
Frontier novels sold best in cities during corporate booms.
Correct: paragraph 3 links the myth to urban anxieties such as crowding and corporations dissolving individual achievement.
Settlers' diaries frequently praised individualism and self-reliance.
That would weaken paragraph 2's contrast between diaries and the later myth.
Frontier myths had little influence on later government land policy.
That contradicts paragraph 4, which says the myths shaped policy.
qs.x: The author argues that frontier myths answer urban anxieties such as crowding and corporations dissolving individual achievement (paragraph 3). City readers buying frontier novels most during corporate growth fits that link directly. Novels written by homesteaders would do the opposite, undercutting paragraph 2's claim that the myth is composed afterward, in cities.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's account of frontier myths?
o: Farmers keep careful ledgers of rainfall and crop prices each season.
This matches the settlers' diaries, not the later myth the author analyzes.
A historian corrects errors in an earlier account of a famous battle using newly discovered letters from soldiers.
The author is not concerned with factual correction but with why a myth was needed.
A village records its own festivals in a locally kept chronicle that is read aloud each year.
Myths in the passage come from the center about the margin, not from the margin itself.
Films romanticizing village life thrive in fast-growing cities during housing shortages.
Correct: like frontier myths, they supply an urban audience with what it fears it lacks (paragraph 3).
qs.x: The core structure is that a settled center produces a romantic story about a margin to supply what it feels it lacks (paragraph 3). City audiences embracing romantic village films during housing shortages share that structure. A village's own chronicle is tempting because it involves village life, but it comes from the margin itself, the opposite of the author's model.

passages.title: The Retreating Mirage
text: Few complaints are as common among travelers as the complaint that a place has been ruined by tourists. The village festival has become a show, the market sells souvenirs made elsewhere, the dancers perform on a schedule printed in the hotel lobby. The traveler who voices this complaint usually exempts himself from the crowd he blames, imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing.

Sociologists have long described the resulting predicament. Hosts, aware that visitors crave authenticity, stage a version of it, arranging back regions that appear private but are designed to be seen. Visitors, sensing the staging, push further in search of something unarranged, and the hosts follow. On this view, authenticity is a mirage that retreats as the tourist approaches, and every encounter is quietly counterfeit.

The analysis is shrewd, but it smuggles in an assumption I find untenable: that a practice performed for outsiders is thereby less genuine than one performed for insiders alone. Cultures have always presented themselves to visitors, and the presentation is itself a cultural act. A dance revived for tourist audiences may be learned by young people who would otherwise have let it lapse, debated by elders over what counts as correct, and altered in ways the community chooses. To call the result fake is to deny the community the right that every culture exercises, the right to change.

The deeper problem lies in the tourist's ideal. The longing for the untouched place casts its residents as inhabitants of the past, people whose value depends on their remaining unlike the visitor. Smartphones in the market, a pop song from a doorway, a guide who studied business administration: these register as intrusions only because the traveler has decided in advance what the place is for. Authenticity, if the word is worth keeping, should describe the relation between a people and their practices, not the match between a destination and a visitor's expectations.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's position?
o: Practices performed for tourists can be authentic; the trouble lies in what tourists expect.
Correct: paragraphs 3 and 4 defend such performances and locate 'the deeper problem' in the tourist's ideal.
Tourism inevitably makes every cultural encounter counterfeit.
That is the sociological view in paragraph 2, which the author challenges.
Authenticity can be found only in places that tourists have not yet reached or changed.
Paragraph 4 criticizes this longing for the untouched place.
Communities should stop performing traditional dances for visitors.
Paragraph 3 suggests such performances can sustain and renew traditions.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that performing for outsiders does not make a practice less genuine, and paragraph 4 places 'the deeper problem' in the tourist's ideal of an untouched place. The claim that every encounter is counterfeit is tempting because the passage presents it, but it is the sociological view the author challenges.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the sociological analysis in paragraph 2 is best described as:
o: wholly dismissive of its account of staged authenticity and back regions.
Calling it 'shrewd' shows the author credits part of it.
fully supportive, since it explains why places are ruined by visitors.
The author rejects its conclusion that every encounter is counterfeit.
indifferent, since it concerns hosts rather than tourists.
The author engages it directly and builds the argument against it.
appreciative of its insight but critical of a hidden assumption.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it 'shrewd' but says it 'smuggles in an assumption I find untenable.'
qs.x: Calling the analysis 'shrewd' credits its insight into staged authenticity, while saying it 'smuggles in an assumption I find untenable' marks the author's disagreement. That mix of credit and criticism rules out both 'wholly dismissive' and 'fully supportive'; attitude questions often hinge on such qualifying words.

qs.q: The example of a dance revived for tourist audiences is used to show that:
o: tourist demand always distorts traditional forms beyond recognition, whatever the community intends.
The example shows changes 'the community chooses,' not distortion imposed from outside.
elders oppose any change to traditional practices.
Elders debate what is correct; the passage does not say they oppose all change.
performing for outsiders can involve real community choice and continuity.
Correct: paragraph 3 notes young people learn it, elders debate it, and the community chooses how it changes.
dances are the only practices tourists find authentic.
The dance is one example, not a claim about tourists' preferences.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a revived dance may be learned by young people, debated by elders and changed 'in ways the community chooses.' The example shows that performing for visitors can involve real choice and continuity. It does not show distortion beyond recognition, since the changes come from the community itself.

qs.q: In noting that the complaining traveler 'exempts himself from the crowd he blames,' the author implies that:
o: solitary travelers are more respectful than tour groups.
The author treats this self-image as an illusion, not a fact.
the complainer shares the very tourist position he criticizes.
Correct: paragraph 1 suggests he is part of the crowd while imagining he alone seeks 'the real thing.'
complaints about tourism are usually accurate.
The author goes on to question the assumptions behind such complaints.
locals blame individual travelers for overcrowding.
The remark concerns the traveler's self-perception, not locals' views.
qs.x: The traveler blames the crowd while 'imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing' (paragraph 1). The author's irony is that he is part of the crowd he criticizes. Taking his self-image at face value, that solo travelers are more respectful, misses that the author presents it as an illusion.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument in paragraph 3?
o: Young residents often learn revived dances to perform them for visitors.
This matches paragraph 3's own example and supports the argument.
Tourist dances are typically choreographed by outside tour firms, excluding residents.
Correct: paragraph 3 rests on the community choosing how the practice changes; outside control would undercut that.
Some tourists prefer performances they believe are unstaged.
Paragraph 2 already assumes tourists crave the unstaged; this adds nothing against paragraph 3.
Residents of tourist towns frequently own smartphones.
This relates to paragraph 4 and does not bear on community control of performances.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's argument depends on the community choosing how a performance changes; that is why it counts as genuine. If outside tour firms choreographed the dances and excluded residents, that support would collapse. Smartphone ownership relates to paragraph 4, not to who controls the performances, so it does not weaken paragraph 3.

passages.title: Legible Hands
text: Every restoration of an old painting rests on an answer, usually unspoken, to a deceptively simple question: what is the painting? For much of the nineteenth century the answer was the image the artist intended, and restorers acted accordingly, repainting lost passages, scrubbing away darkened varnish, and occasionally 'improving' a composition they judged clumsy. The results were often handsome and nearly always irreversible. A restorer confident that he knew what the master meant had no reason to leave a trace of himself.

The reaction against this confidence produced its own orthodoxy. Critics began to celebrate patina, the yellowed varnish and fine cracking that time lays over a canvas, as an integral part of the work. To clean a painting, on this view, was to erase its biography. But the cult of patina is no more modest than the cult of intention; it merely transfers authority from the artist to the centuries, and it can license neglect as easily as the older view licensed overpainting. A varnish so dark that the figures beneath it are illegible does not preserve a history. It conceals one.

I would propose a different answer. A painting is both an image and a document, and restoration ought to respect the second role without abandoning the first. This is the logic behind the Italian practice of tratteggio, in which losses are filled with fine vertical hatching that blends into the surrounding paint at a normal viewing distance but reveals itself on close inspection. The viewer sees a coherent picture; the scholar sees exactly where the original stops.

The principle can be stated simply: an intervention should be legible and, wherever possible, reversible. Legibility admits that the restorer is a later hand, working with later knowledge and later taste. Reversibility admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded. Neither principle tells us how far to clean a particular picture, and honest conservators will continue to disagree about that. What the principles rule out is the pretense that any restoration can be invisible, as though the painting had simply been returned to a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen.

qs.q: According to the passage, tratteggio is valuable because it:
o: restores a painting exactly to the artist's original intention
Paragraph 4 denies any restoration can return a work to its original moment.
preserves the darkened varnish that records a painting's age
Tratteggio fills losses; Paragraph 3 says nothing about keeping varnish.
allows restorers to correct compositional flaws in the original
'Improving' compositions is the nineteenth-century practice Paragraph 1 criticizes.
blends in at viewing distance yet shows its boundaries up close
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the hatching blends at normal distance but reveals itself on close inspection.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 describes tratteggio as hatching that blends into the picture at normal distance but shows itself up close, so viewers get a coherent image and scholars see where the original ends. This serves the author's view that a painting is both image and document. It does not restore original intention, which Paragraph 4 says no restoration can do.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the 'cult of patina' is that it:
o: hands authority to time and can excuse neglect
Correct: Paragraph 2 says it 'transfers authority from the artist to the centuries' and can 'license neglect.'
encourages restorers to repaint lost passages of the original in their own style
Repainting belongs to the cult of intention in Paragraph 1, not the cult of patina.
relies on chemical methods that damage the canvas
Paragraph 2 raises no technical or chemical objection.
treats the painting as a document rather than an image
The author endorses the document view in Paragraph 3; the objection to patina is different.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the cult of patina is 'no more modest' than the cult of intention: it simply moves authority from the artist to the centuries and can excuse leaving a painting illegible. Repainting lost passages belongs to the nineteenth-century intention view in Paragraph 1, so attributing it to patina confuses the two orthodoxies the author criticizes.

qs.q: The final phrase, 'a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen,' suggests that:
o: old paintings were rarely displayed when they were first made
Paragraph 4 makes no claim about original display practices.
restorers should consult eyewitness accounts of original works before cleaning them
The point of Paragraph 4 is that no such witnesses exist, not that they should be consulted.
a painting's original appearance is not directly known to anyone today
Correct: Paragraph 4 says claims to restore the original moment are a pretense, since no one has seen it.
modern viewers lack the taste to appreciate old paintings
Paragraph 4 concerns knowledge of appearance, not the quality of modern taste.
qs.x: The closing phrase says the 'original moment' a restorer claims to return to has never been seen by anyone alive, so the painting's first appearance is not directly known. That is why invisible restoration is a pretense. The eyewitness choice misreads the point: the author stresses that no such witnesses exist, not that they should be consulted.

qs.q: The author's call for reversible restoration depends most on which assumption?
o: Original paint is always more valuable than restorers' additions.
Paragraph 4 bases reversibility on future knowledge, not a ranking of paint.
Later conservators may know things that make present choices look wrong.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says reversibility 'admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded.'
Most viewers can easily tell restored passages from the original paint around them.
Paragraph 3 says tratteggio blends in at normal distance, so viewers often cannot tell.
Patina is the most important record of a painting's history and must never be removed.
Paragraph 2 criticizes the cult of patina, so this is not the author's premise.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 justifies reversibility by saying it 'admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded': later conservators may know better and need to undo present work. The assumption is about the fallibility of current knowledge. The choice that viewers can spot restorations contradicts Paragraph 3, where tratteggio blends in at normal distance.

qs.q: A museum repaints a damaged face so seamlessly that experts cannot find the repair even under magnification, but uses a paint that can be fully removed. The author would most likely:
o: praise the repair because it restores the artist's intended image
Paragraph 1 rejects the confidence that restorers know the intended image.
reject the repair because any filling of losses is improper
Paragraph 3 endorses filling losses through tratteggio, so filling is not itself improper.
accept the repair fully, since it can be undone later
Paragraph 4 requires legibility as well as reversibility; this repair is not legible.
approve its reversibility but object to its look
Correct: Paragraph 4 requires interventions to be legible and reversible; this meets only one test.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 sets two tests: an intervention should be legible and, where possible, reversible. A repair no expert can find even under magnification passes the reversibility test but fails legibility, since it pretends to be invisible. Full acceptance is the tempting trap; it ignores that reversibility alone does not satisfy the author's principle.

qs.q: Which discovery would most strengthen the author's criticism of nineteenth-century restoration?
o: A famous 'improvement' rested on a misreading, but cannot be removed without harm.
Correct: it shows the danger Paragraph 1 notes, confident changes that are irreversible.
Some nineteenth-century restorers kept detailed records of their work, including what they repainted.
Good records would soften, not strengthen, the critique of leaving no trace in Paragraph 1.
Darkened varnish slowly damages the paint layer beneath it.
This bears on the patina debate in Paragraph 2, not on nineteenth-century overpainting.
Modern viewers prefer cleaned paintings to uncleaned ones when shown both side by side.
Viewer preference does not address the irreversibility the author criticizes in Paragraph 1.
qs.x: The author faults nineteenth-century restorers for confident changes that were 'nearly always irreversible' and left no trace. Finding that a celebrated 'improvement' rested on a misreading and cannot be safely removed shows both flaws causing real harm. Detailed records would soften the critique, and varnish damage concerns the separate patina debate.

passages.title: The Unfair Persuader
text: Defenders of advertising aimed at children usually make two arguments. Advertising, they say, is a form of speech that informs consumers about products, and parents, who control the household budget, stand between the child and any purchase. Both arguments assume a listener who can recognize persuasion as persuasion. Developmental research suggests that this assumption fails for young children: many children under about eight treat commercials as a kind of entertainment or as neutral information, not as messages designed by someone who wants their money.

The case against child-directed advertising is often made on grounds of harm, by linking advertisements to sugary diets or to materialism. Those links are real but contested, and I think they are not the heart of the matter. The deeper wrong lies in an asymmetry. A persuasive message aimed at a person who cannot identify its purpose is closer to manipulation than to argument, because the listener cannot weigh the message against the motive behind it. Even if a child's newfound craving for a cereal led to no harm at all, the exchange would be defective in the way a swindle is defective even when the victim happens to lose nothing.

The parental-gatekeeper defense fares no better. The industry's own term for one of its strategies, “pester power,” reveals the plan: rather than persuading the parent, the advertiser recruits the child as an advocate inside the home. A defense that names parents as the filter cannot easily survive a marketing practice designed to go around them.

I concede that the line is blurry. Older children and teenagers recognize the intent of advertising and yet remain susceptible to it. Recognition, then, is necessary for fair persuasion but not sufficient. For adolescents, the case for restriction must lean on harm-based arguments, which I regard as relevant but less decisive. Yet newer formats complicate even this concession. Sponsored unboxing videos and branded games erase the boundary between content and commercial on which older children depend to recognize a sales pitch. Such formats, I suggest, return older children to the protected class from which their maturity had seemed to remove them.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central thesis?
o: Advertising to children is wrong mainly because it reliably causes unhealthy eating.
Paragraph 2 calls harm links real but contested and says they are not the heart of the matter.
Advertising to young children is wrong chiefly because it targets people who cannot recognize its intent.
Correct: paragraph 2 locates the deeper wrong in this asymmetry, which makes the message closer to manipulation.
Parents should be held fully responsible for whatever advertisements their children watch on television or online.
Paragraph 3 argues the parental-gatekeeper defense fails, so the author does not place full responsibility on parents.
All advertising directed at people under eighteen should be banned on equal grounds.
Paragraph 4 says the case for adolescents rests on weaker, harm-based grounds, so the grounds are not equal.
qs.x: The thesis sits in paragraph 2: the deeper wrong is an asymmetry, since a child who cannot recognize persuasive intent cannot weigh the message against the motive. The harm-based option is tempting, but the author explicitly calls harm links real but contested and not the heart of the matter.

qs.q: The author mentions the industry term “pester power” primarily in order to:
o: show that children are more persuasive than adults realize.
Paragraph 3 uses the term to expose a strategy, not to praise children's persuasive skill.
argue that advertisers have become more honest about their methods.
The author treats the term as revealing, not as evidence of growing honesty or reform.
suggest that parents are to blame for giving in to their children.
Paragraph 3 faults the advertiser's strategy for routing around parents, not the parents themselves.
undermine the claim that parents serve as an effective filter between child and advertiser.
Correct: paragraph 3 says a defense naming parents as the filter cannot survive a practice designed to bypass them.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 quotes the industry's own phrase to turn it against the industry: a strategy built to recruit children as advocates is designed to bypass parents. That undercuts the gatekeeper defense. Blaming parents is the trap; the author faults the advertiser's plan, not the parents who are routed around.

qs.q: The comparison to a swindle in paragraph 2 serves to illustrate that:
o: a persuasive exchange can wrong someone without harm.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the exchange would be defective even if the craving led to no harm, as with a harmless swindle.
children who see advertisements typically lose money or possessions as a result.
The analogy stresses the victim losing nothing, so it does not claim children lose money.
advertisers knowingly commit crimes that should be prosecuted.
The author draws a moral parallel, not a legal claim about prosecution.
harm-based arguments are the strongest case against advertising.
Paragraph 2 sets harm aside as not the heart of the matter, the opposite of this claim.
qs.x: A swindle is wrong because of how it treats the victim, even if the victim happens to lose nothing. Paragraph 2 uses this to show the author's objection does not depend on harm. Reading it as a claim that children lose money reverses the analogy's point.

qs.q: Which new finding would most weaken the author's argument regarding young children?
o: Children exposed to more food advertising consume slightly more sugar.
This supports a harm argument, which the author already treats as secondary, and does not touch the main premise.
Teenagers who recognize advertising intent still buy advertised products about as often as younger children do.
Paragraph 4 already concedes that recognition does not end susceptibility in older children.
Most children as young as four can reliably explain that commercials try to make people buy things.
Correct: the argument rests on young children failing to recognize persuasive intent, and this finding removes that premise.
Parents report frequent arguments with their children over toys the children saw advertised on television.
This fits the pester-power point in paragraph 3 rather than weakening the argument.
qs.x: To weaken an argument, attack its key premise. Paragraph 1's premise is that young children do not recognize persuasive intent, and the whole manipulation argument rests on it. Evidence about teenagers or sugar intake touches only claims the author already concedes or treats as secondary.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely regard an undisclosed video in which a popular host plays with toys supplied by their maker as:
o: acceptable for older children, since they understand advertising intent.
Paragraph 4 says such formats return older children to the protected class, so they are not exempt.
harmless as long as no purchase follows from viewing it.
Paragraph 2 says an unfair persuasive exchange is defective even without harm or loss.
less troubling than a standard commercial, because it does not directly ask any viewer to make a purchase.
The author sees blurred formats as worse, because hiding the pitch defeats recognition.
especially objectionable, because it hides the persuasive intent that older children rely on detecting.
Correct: paragraph 4 says such formats erase the content-commercial boundary older children need.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says hidden formats such as sponsored videos erase the content-commercial boundary that older children use to spot a pitch, putting them back in the protected class. So concealment makes the case worse, not better. The older-children option ignores this; the harmless option ignores paragraph 2's point that harmlessness does not cure unfairness.

qs.q: Which best describes the author's attitude toward harm-based arguments against child-directed advertising?
o: They are irrelevant and should be abandoned by critics of advertising.
Paragraph 4 calls them relevant, so the author does not dismiss them as irrelevant.
They matter but are less decisive than unrecognized intent.
Correct: paragraph 2 calls the harm links real but contested, and paragraph 4 calls them relevant but less decisive.
They are conclusive for young children but irrelevant for adolescents.
The author relies on harm arguments mainly for adolescents, the reverse of this description.
They are stronger than the manipulation argument once complete data on children's health are available.
The author never ranks harm above the asymmetry argument, which paragraph 2 calls the deeper wrong.
qs.x: The author keeps harm arguments in play, calling them relevant (paragraph 4), but ranks them below the unrecognized-intent argument, which paragraph 2 calls the deeper wrong. Calling them irrelevant overstates the author's dismissal; the author leans on them for adolescents.
